Think of a huge old apartment building where everyone in the world lives, thousands of floors, every door with a name on it.

There is no front desk, no manager, no one in charge of the whole building. Nobody owns it.

If you want to give something to a neighbor, you write their name on it. You hand it to the person in the hallway. That person doesn't know where your neighbor lives — they only know which direction to pass it: *up*, or *down*, or *toward the river side*. So they hand it to someone a little closer. That one does the same. The note gets passed up the stairs, across landings, past dogs and cooking smells, until someone finally says, "That name lives here," and slides it under the door.

That's the whole internet.

Two things make it work.

The first is that nothing travels whole. If you want to send someone a long letter, it gets torn into small numbered pieces, and each piece travels its own way — one up the north stairs, one through the back corridor, one out the roof and down the other side — and they arrive out of order, by different people, at different times. There's a number on each piece, so your neighbor lays them out and reads them in the right order. If one piece is lost, they send a note back that just says "number seven," and it gets passed again. That's why nothing needs to be perfect or careful. It only needs to be patient.

The second is the names. Every door has one, and they're all different. That's the only reason any of this works. It isn't a smart building — it's a building where everyone agreed, long ago, that no two people would share a name, and everyone kept the agreement even though it's no one's job to enforce it.

And here's the strange part, the part worth sitting with: nobody in the building knows the layout. Not a single person. The person who hands your note to the next person has never seen the floor it's going to. The whole building moves billions of these slips of paper a day, upstairs and downstairs, without one person alive holding the map. It is held together by nothing but a shared habit of passing things along.

If that sounds fragile — it is. Pieces get lost, notes arrive late, sometimes a whole hallway goes dark and the paper goes around it, and nobody upstairs ever learns it happened.

Now, one more thing, and this is the part that's hard to fit in the building.

There are rooms in it that are not apartments. There's a room filled with nothing but the names of everyone, written in a giant book, so you can look up where anyone lives — but the book is copied and recopied across dozens of floors, and they argue constantly about which copy is right.

And there are rooms where you can't visit, only ask. You write your question, slide it under the door, and someone inside — you'll never meet them, you'll never know their name — writes the answer and slides it back. A shop with no shopkeeper. A house that answers.

That's the internet. Not a place. Not a machine. A habit that a few billion strangers keep, of passing each other's paper in the right direction, without ever being told how.

Think of a small town, but not the kind with a main street. Imagine a town with no center and no downtown, where everyone keeps a small wooden box by their front door, and a stack of blank cards and a pen inside.

Suppose you want to send a message to your friend. You could have something in your box. You take out a card and write what you want to say. But a real message is not a short thing, and in this town, a card fits only one word. So the message goes onto many cards, one small piece per card, and each card gets a number and the address of the friend at the top.

Now, the cards do not go in one bundle. The system of this town spreads them out. One card goes over the bridge. Another goes by the field. Another goes through the market square. Some of the cards take a long road and some take a short one, and they will not arrive in the same order and they may not arrive on the same day. What matters is that your friend's box gets every card, and that the numbers are at the top of each one, so your friend can lay them out on the floor and put them in order and see the message whole.

The whole town is built on a few agreements, and nothing else holds it together. You agree that card number three is the third piece of the message. You agree on a number for each friend. You agree that the cards you are willing to carry, you will carry, and that the ones you cannot, you will pass to whoever is standing next to you.

But the town is not just this one town. A card, if it is going to someone in another town, is not carried by hand. You put it in the box, and the box does not shelter the card. It goes to a place that has a set of roads, and one of those roads leads to the next town, and that next town has its own boxes and its own roads, and the card is carried through the crossing points, and no one is reading the whole message at any point.

The thing that makes it worked is not that a person with a great memory knows the way to everyone. The system is not a route. It is a rule for the way we label the cards. It's also a shared idea: if you and I both number the cards the same way, and each of us uses the shared addresses of the whole town, the cards can travel along any roads at all.

Now the thing that makes today's world different from the earlier towns is not a single big machine in the sky. There is no single big box. There is a set of boxes that can take a set of cards and pass them through the crossing points, and roadworks, and the roads of daily commerce that are all the time carrying cards. The difference is that the roads never stop, and the crossing points are not a town: each crossing point only knows the next place it is sending a card. It does not know what message is in your hand, only the way to the next crossing.

The last part is the part that people miss. The whole thing is a whole world's worth of just a single agreement. The small town, before this, could send a message. But it could not send a voice to a person across the ocean, and it could not send a photograph at the same instant and then the same road and the same rules all over the world. In the old town, the card was the same whether you were sending it to the house next to you or to a house a thousand miles away. The rule that says "the card is the message, not the road" is the whole of the internet. It isn't held up by any one thing. It is held up by the fact that everyone carries the same rules. There is no castle. The only thing the whole thing rests on is the agreement, which is the closest thing we have to the fact that a town can be a town without a center.

# The Gap

Her name is Oda Reyes and she is an electrician. People get this wrong about her in one of two directions, and both of them are a way of not listening. The first: how nice, a lady sparky. The second: how useful, they'll need a woman on set who can check the wiring. Oda doesn't work on sets. She works on houses that have started to misbehave — a light that comes on at three in the morning in a room nobody has entered since March, a freezer that runs all night without generating a single degree of cold, a breaker that stays closed for a week and then gets tired and opens.

The thing Oda knows, the thing she cannot stop knowing, is that a house is a witness that never gets interviewed. Every wire in a wall is a record of a decision somebody made about where things should be. Somebody had to open the plaster. Somebody had to buy the copper. Somebody had to decide the kitchen light came back on the same circuit as the outlet in the hall, and that person had opinions about how the house should behave, and those opinions are still there, sixty years later, humming at fifty hertz, wanting things.

The police call her three times a year. Not because she is clever. Because she is the last person who saw the wiring the way it was before. Nobody photographs a house from inside its own walls. Oda does. She has eleven thousand photographs on a drive in her basement, every one of them of something you would have to cut open a house to see, each with a date and an address and a note she wrote for herself because she did not know, yet, what it was going to matter to. She finds the extension cord that runs from a bedroom across two rooms and out through a hole in the floor — somebody needed to run a space heater from a dead outlet, or somebody needed a lamp near a door so a person could see to leave — and she does not know which. She says so. This is what makes her hard to use.

Oda is fifty-one and she is not a detective and she has no gift, except one that many electricians have and most never name. When the breaker trips, she does not look at the breaker. She listens and thinks about what the house is trying to tell her, and then she starts removing drywall in the least likely places. She can hear a splice through plaster, or a staple driven too close to a conductor, because she has spent thirty years putting her hand on the surface of things and learning what each one is hiding. It is a real skill. It is not magic. It is the sort of thing that will get you named in court if you're careless about what you say it proves.

Now the part that costs her. For twenty years she has refused to give an opinion about guilt. Her reports list what a wire was carrying, where it went, when it was installed, and the date she found it — and then she stops. This has made her a reputation, and the reputation has lately begun to pay badly, because a murder case needs a person who's willing to say what the evidence means. She is being handed the same case she almost got stuck to, once, and she knows it. She can feel it the way she can feel a bad splice: that fine grit in her teeth before the light goes. She wants the phone to stop. She wants to be the kind of person who says what she thinks and takes the consequence, instead of the kind of person who photographs everything and interprets nothing, who leaves the whole ugly shape of it for somebody else to assemble, who has spent her life standing in other people's walls, holding her breath, never once in a room she chose.

In the first chapter she is called to a house where something has been disturbed and the police already have their story. Someone has sewn a little extra into the walls. She knows because she has the same room on her drive from four years ago, and it doesn't match. It is the sort of discrepancy a prosecutor would love and a defense attorney would kill, and it is three feet to the left of the thing everyone is looking at.

She has three choices. Report the difference and let the case run the way cases run, and live with the door she opened. Keep filling the drive and fill it again when this house is emptied and sold to people who will never know what it was. Or open a wall she was told not to open, in a house she has no call to be in, and find out what she wants badly enough to break her own rule for.

She is going to open the wall. That is the book. She will be wrong about why she opened it, and she will be wrong about what's behind it, and the thing she is actually looking for — the thing that has run hidden in her own walls since she was a girl in a house with a bad ground — will turn out to be the case itself. She is not a detective discovering a killer. She is a woman learning to say what she means.

- Brief: unusual protagonist for a mystery. They did not specify genre-era, length, or whether they want a list or a character sketch. I'll build one character, fully formed.
- Default to dodge: the detective on the cover of every book in the section — heavy drinker, insomniac, forensic eye, dead wife behind him; the 21st-century coat of paint is the quirky consultant with an eidetic memory or a synesthesia that renders clues in color.
- Second-order tells to dodge too: the animal narrating, the AI detective, the seven-item list of charming quirks, the dead girl as victim, the protagonist who is secretly the villain.
- What I have to stand on: a mystery is a machine for "who did it," and the thing I'm looking for should be the *engine* of that question, not decoration bolted onto a cop.
- Direction A (lens — wrong expert): an electrician. Not a genius — a woman whose trade is the truth of what happens inside a wall when nobody's watching, following current, finding the grounds.
- Direction B (form — borrowed vessel): a probation officer's file; too talky.
- Direction C (premise — assumption reversal): the witness everyone has already convicted. Too close to the "wrongly accused" fog.
- Direction D (subtraction — remove the center): a professional witness with no stake in either story.
- I'll go with the electrician, but keep it from being a cosy-trade gimmick: her competence should generate pressure on the plot, not a warm quirk. Her flaw should cost her something real.

<final>
# The Gap

Her name is Oda Reyes and she is an electrician. People get this wrong about her in one of two directions, and both of them are a way of not listening. The first: how nice, a lady sparky. The second: how useful, they'll need a woman on set who can check the wiring. Oda doesn't work on sets. She works on houses that have started to misbehave — a light that comes on at three in the morning in a room nobody has entered since March, a freezer that runs all night without generating a single degree of cold, a breaker that stays closed for a week and then gets tired and opens.

The thing Oda knows, the thing she cannot stop knowing, is that a house is a witness that never gets interviewed. Every wire in a wall is a record of a decision somebody made about where things should be. Somebody had to open the plaster. Somebody had to buy the copper. Somebody had to decide the kitchen light came back on the same circuit as the outlet in the hall, and that person had opinions about how the house should behave, and those opinions are still there, sixty years later, humming at fifty hertz, wanting things.

The police call her three times a year. Not because she is clever. Because she is the last person who saw the wiring the way it was before. Nobody photographs a house from inside its own walls. Oda does. She has eleven thousand photographs on a drive in her basement, every one of them of something you would have to cut open a house to see, each with a date and an address and a note she wrote for herself because she did not know, yet, what it was going to matter to. She finds the extension cord that runs from a bedroom across two rooms and out through a hole in the floor — somebody needed to run a space heater from a dead outlet, or somebody needed a lamp near a door so a person could see to leave — and she does not know which. She says so. This is what makes her hard to use.

Oda is fifty-one and she is not a detective and she has no gift, except one that many electricians have and most never name. When the breaker trips, she does not look at the breaker. She listens and thinks about what the house is trying to tell her, and then she starts removing drywall in the least likely places. She can hear a splice through plaster, or a staple driven too close to a conductor, because she has spent thirty years putting her hand on the surface of things and learning what each one is hiding. It is a real skill. It is not magic. It is the sort of thing that will get you named in court if you're careless about what you say it proves.

Now the part that costs her. For twenty years she has refused to give an opinion about guilt. Her reports list what a wire was carrying, where it went, when it was installed, and the date she found it — and then she stops. This has made her a reputation, and the reputation has lately begun to pay badly, because a murder case needs a person who's willing to say what the evidence means. She is being handed the same case she almost got stuck to, once, and she knows it. She can feel it the way she can feel a bad splice: that fine grit in her teeth before the light goes. She wants the phone to stop. She wants to be the kind of person who says what she thinks and takes the consequence, instead of the kind of person who photographs everything and interprets nothing, who leaves the whole ugly shape of it for somebody else to assemble, who has spent her life standing in other people's walls, holding her breath, never once in a room she chose.

In the first chapter she is called to a house where something has been disturbed and the police already have their story. Someone has sewn a little extra into the walls. She knows because she has the same room on her drive from four years ago, and it doesn't match. It is the sort of discrepancy a prosecutor would love and a defense attorney would kill, and it is three feet to the left of the thing everyone is looking at.

She has three choices. Report the difference and let the case run the way cases run, and live with the door she opened. Keep filling the drive and fill it again when this house is emptied and sold to people who will never know what it was. Or open a wall she was told not to open, in a house she has no call to be in, and find out what she wants badly enough to break her own rule for.

She is going to open the wall. That is the book. She will be wrong about why she opened it, and she will be wrong about what's behind it, and the thing she is actually looking for — the thing that has run hidden in her own walls since she was a girl in a house with a bad ground — will turn out to be the case itself. She is not a detective discovering a killer. She is a woman learning to say what she means.
</final>

One assumption: no era or tone was specified, so I wrote it as contemporary and slightly hard-boiled. If you want it gentler, or set somewhere the houses are older, both are easy to steer.

**Deep Water**

Nothing here has seen the sun.
The water is old and holds its cold
the way a mouth holds a coin.

Down past the last blue
there is no blue.
There are things that make their own light
and pay for it with hunger,
and things that wait,
which is the same as making light
if you wait long enough.

The bottom is not a floor.
It is a kind of weather,
slow, that moves a mile in a thousand years
and takes the bones of whales
and keeps them in the dark
like a hand closing.

Most of the world is this.
You have been standing on the roof
of a house with one lit room
and calling it the sea.

Default: rhymed quatrains, "O ocean" address, dancing waves, golden sun, silver moon, closing stanza that states the theme; or the second-order move — the ocean narrates itself. Both are defaults. Anchor: the true fact that the deep sea is the planet's largest habitat and almost nobody pictures it. final: A down-on-his-luck barrister in a city where magic is a nonrenewable resource apportioned by contract gets handed the worst case of his career: a widow wants to claw back her late husband's allotment, which he willed — every year of it, down to the last spark — to a stranger. The catch is that a will can't give away what the dead don't own. Whoever inherits the man's magic inherits his debts, his vows, his marriage, and every promise made with it, which is why nobody with a clean record wants the widow to win. He takes the case anyway, mostly out of guilt, and finds himself suing the man's memory on behalf of the people who spent thirty years living it. The trial runs long. The stranger's side keeps calling witnesses who cry. Nobody, in the end, gets the magic; everybody gets the man.

Quick notes: Default is a chosen-one orphan, a dark lord or prophecy, a quest map, medieval-Europe-flavored setting. I'm flipping the quietly doubtful assumption — in fantasy, magic is scarce and hoarded from the powerful. Here it's the opposite: the supply is fixed, ruled by contract law, and everyone is entangled. Genre transposition into contract law, not a war.

The badge machine was still in the box. Denise had watched them uncrate it from the loading bay two years ago and had never been given the code to the room it lived in, so on Monday she stood in the corridor holding the door for a man in a coat who did not know her name and did not know he was the reason she was here.

"Marcus," he said. "IT."

"Denise. I'm—" She looked at the door, which was propped with a chair. "I'm sort of the one who knows where things are."

This was true for about six more hours. The office had been sold in March and the lease ran out on Friday, and the man from the acquiring company was due at ten to walk the floor with a clipboard and decide what was worth keeping. Denise had been asked to stay on for the week to make the handover smooth. She had been asked this in a meeting where someone used the word "legacy," and she had said yes because it was easier than saying no, and because her desk still had her plants on it.

Marcus could not find the badge machine's code, so she took him to the second floor and showed him the drawer where Rob kept the spare fobs and the drawer where Rob kept the spare batteries and the drawer where Rob kept the things nobody would admit to keeping. Rob had been gone since April. She had not cleaned out his drawers. It seemed like a job for someone with more authority than she had, and then there was no one with more authority, and then it was Monday.

"This is a lot of drawers," Marcus said.

"He was here eighteen years."

She gave him the fob for the east entrance and the code for the printers and the name of the woman on the fourth floor who would sign for packages if you asked her before lunch. She gave him the trick with the kettle, which only boiled if you pressed the button twice. She did not give him the trick with the photocopier because she did not know it, and neither had anyone else, and the copier had been making that noise since before she arrived.

At ten the man with the clipboard came. He was younger than Denise and wore a lanyard from a conference she had never attended. He walked the floor with Marcus and asked what each room was for. Denise followed a step behind and answered when Marcus could not, and by the third room she understood that she was being interviewed without being asked a question. The clipboard man wrote things down. He looked at the ceiling tiles and the server cupboard and the whiteboard where someone had drawn a graph in 2019 and never wiped it. He said "we'll see" about the server cupboard and "interesting" about the whiteboard.

Marcus found her at lunch in the kitchen, waiting for the kettle to boil twice.

"They're keeping the third floor," he said. "The rest goes dark by Friday."

"I know."

"You don't seem upset."

She thought about how to say it. The truth was that she had been upset in February, when the email came. By Monday she had gotten used to the shape of it. It was the plants she kept thinking about, and whether the movers would let her take them, and whether the third floor had windows.

"There's a folder in the top drawer of my desk," she said. "It has the passwords. The real ones. Rob's system was not good."

Marcus looked at her for a moment. "You could have kept that," he said. "You could have walked out on Friday and let them figure it out."

She poured the water. The kettle had boiled on the second press. "I know," she said. "But he's going to be sitting at my desk on Monday and he's going to be the one who can't find the spare batteries. Someone had to show him the drawer."

By three the clipboard man had gone. By four Marcus had the badge machine open and was reading the manual aloud to himself in a voice she recognized, the voice of a man who has decided to be useful. She finished clearing her desk and found that she had less than she expected. Three plants. A mug. A card from 2017 signed by people whose names she could no longer put to faces. The folder she left in the drawer, with a note on the front that said *Rob's system. Sorry. Start with the batteries.*

She carried the plants down in two trips. On the second trip she passed the third floor and looked in and saw that it had windows. Marcus was still up there, fitting the badge machine to the wall, and he waved at her through the glass without breaking the rhythm of the drill. She waved back with her free hand. Then she went down to the car park and put the plants in the boot and drove home in the light that was left.

Planning notes (not shown to user):

- Brief: short story, first day at a new job. Open audience, open tone, no length or voice fixed. Intensity: bold (default).
- Default: nervous newcomer arrives, is overwhelmed, makes a small mistake, is rescued by a kind colleague, ends with a hopeful small image. Opening on the commute or the lobby. Stock names.
- Directions weighed:
  1. Premise/stakes relocation: the first day is not the narrator's first day — it's the job's first day; the narrator is the one who has been there longest and is now the last one left of the old team. Anchor: "new job" can mean new to the person or new to the company. Risk: might read as gimmick.
  2. Lens/inverted stake: the first day told by the person whose job is to train the newcomer, and the real event is that she is being made redundant on the same day. Anchor: someone always has to onboard the replacement. Risk: too neat a twist.
  3. Material/specificity: the first day rendered entirely through the objects that get handed over — keys, badge, a mug — and what each one reveals about the place. Anchor: a first day is mostly a sequence of handovers. Risk: could turn into a list.
- Chose 1, with the material discipline of 3 and the human friction of 2 kept as texture: the narrator is the outgoing one who shows the newcomer around, and the tension is that the office is being emptied on the same day. Reason: it grows from the ambiguity in "new job" and lets the day carry real stakes without inflating them. It also avoids the "kind colleague rescues nervous newcomer" default and the "twist" default by putting the turn early, not at the end.
- Keep the ending un-summarizing: no sunrise, no single hopeful image, no lesson.

The sea keeps no ledger of the ships it has swallowed.
It returns the rope, the bottle, the single boot,
then sends the boot back again, as if to ask
whether you meant to lose it.

At low tide the shore is a bookkeeper,
laying out every shell it has been handed,
tallying the crab-legs and the glass,
never once asking who left them.

I think of my grandmother's kitchen drawer,
all twine and dead batteries and keys
to doors that were sold before I was born.
The ocean is that drawer, the whole of it,
and nothing in it is ever thrown away.

The tide does not ask the shore
what it wants to keep.
It takes the glass, the bootprint,
the name somebody scratched in sand
and hands back the whelk
with its door still shut.

All night the water counts the stones
and loses its place,
starts over, and loses it again.
Out past the buoy
a light blinks four times,
waits for an answer,
gets only the sea.

I used to think the ocean was big
because it had so much to hold.
Now I think it is big
because it never once
has been finished with anything.

**The Ocean Takes the Job No One Else Will**

The ocean is a laborer.
It hauls the same grey rope all night
and never asks what it is for.
It keeps the buoys, it salts the wood,
it sorts the kelp into piles nobody wants.

I have seen it carry a whole sky
on its back and not complain,
seen it take the wind's bad temper
and answer with a shrug of foam.

They say it is deep.
They say it is a mother.
I have watched it drop a boat
and go back to its work.

At dusk it buys a little light off the sun
and spends it all on the horizon,
a poor man at a market
holding up coins to the last stall.

I asked it once what it was thinking.
It showed me a crab, a bottle, a bone.
Meaning: this is the inventory.
Meaning: I keep what comes.
Meaning: I am not hiding anything,
you just cannot read it.

I have stopped asking permission
to stand at its edge and be small.
It does not want my fear.
It does not want my praise.

It wants the next wave
lined up behind this one,
the next tide,
the next thousand years of the same
steady, thankless, shining work.

And when it stands up in the wind
and drags its nails across the sand —
that is not grief.
That is the sound of something
that has never once
been allowed to stop.

Brief notes:
- Fixed parts: it’s a poem, about the ocean. Open otherwise. No length, voice, or form given.
- Default version: moon/June rhymes, “O ocean,” waves as breathing/heartbeat, the sea as a mirror of the soul, closing with a nod to eternity. Stock images: crashing waves, salt spray, gulls, deep mystery, “the boundless deep.”
- Trigger: “poem about the ocean” is one of the most heavily defaulted briefs there is. The task is to keep the thing genuinely a poem about the ocean — real ocean, real feeling — while refusing the greeting-card sea.
- Direction chosen: not the sea as scenery or metaphor for the soul, but the sea as *laborer, keeper, buoy*. Give it a working voice and a ledger of what it does all day with no reward and no witness. Keep it concrete: rubber, rope, kelp, shade, a bell bought at a marine store, a voice that doesn’t hold a tune. The ocean’s indifference is the real odd fact — it is the one huge thing that does not care whether we are here, and that is its beauty. Keep the poem’s pull: a voice, a small narrative, and a change (from “tell me” to “I stopped asking permission”).
- Guardrail: no abstract nouns doing the work, no “O Ocean,” no closing lesson. End on work, not wisdom.

The ocean

Nobody taught it to keep
going. It was going.

Somewhere under it, a light
that was never switched on.

I have watched it work
the same shore for hours
and it does not tire
and it does not finish.

What I remember best
is not the size.
It is that it was cold
and would not stay
in my hand.

Notes:
- Brief: poem, ocean. Fixed: poem form. Open: premise, angle, shape, material, voice. Thin brief, short piece → make one stated assumption (I'll assume a human reader, not a specific occasion) and write.
- Default: waves, moon, tide, "O ocean", vastness, awe, god's grandeur, closing stanza stating theme. Stock material: whisper, dance, silver, deep blue, eternity.
- Second-order default to avoid: personified ocean narrating, or "the ocean as grief/memory."
- Technique families: try Material (specificity + true odd fact) and Subtraction (remove the expected center — the poem never addresses the ocean, never says "sea/ocean").
- Anchor: real, checkable detail — the ocean's loudest sound (the deep sea is loud, but it's biological; and the tide is a slow flexing; the moon pulls water, not the ocean). Pick: the ocean is a body that is mostly in the dark and mostly moving at once, and it does not have a surface meaning.
- Shape: start mid-motion, no apostrophe, end without summing. Keep a body/physical scale.

Draft, then check: swap test (could this fit any subject? tie to water/body/physics specifically), tells (no moon/heart/soul/whisper), payoff (one image that lands).

The checklist came up on the wall screen at 06:00 station time, which was a clock everyone on the ground had agreed to keep for the crew's benefit, and the crew was one person.

Vega floated with one hand on the grab bar by the galley, watching the list write itself. Twelve lines today. It never wrote more than fourteen.

GALLEY FILTER — SWAP CARTRIDGE
WATER RECLAIM #1 — FLOAT TEST
MODULE 2 HATCH SEAL — VISUAL
GALLEY FILTER — SWAP CARTRIDGE

The fourth line was the second line again. Vega had told the ground this three months ago. The ground had said thank you, we'll pass it along. The list had gone on repeating itself the way it always did, and Vega had stopped flagging it, and now those were the two most honest sentences in the station: the machine repeating, the human pretending not to notice.

They had met the others, once. Six of them at the hatch, before the launch that put Vega up here and the rest back on rotation — a handshake, a photo, a real conversation about a sister's wedding and someone's terrible truck. Then the elevators closed and the mission planners did what planners do, which was to discover that the station ran perfectly well with a crew of one. Everything that needed a body, a robot arm could do. Everything that needed a decision, a model could make. What was left for a person was to be present in case something unprecedented happened, and nothing unprecedented had happened in nine months, and Vega was getting very, very good at the galley filter.

You could not swap the cartridge in gloves. The little bay was two hand-widths deep, and the seals were fine, and if you tore one you would vent the galley into the cold for maybe four seconds before the shutoff, which was survivable, and which no model wanted to be blamed for. So it was a human job. It was the human job.

Vega unpacked the new cartridge from its sleeve. It smelled like nothing, which was its own kind of smell up here, where everything else smelled like ozone, hot metal and the inside of the sleeping bag. The bay opened with a click that Vega heard through a fingertip. The old cartridge came out gray and furred with things that had been living in the water.

"Say what you did," Vega said to it.

"Recycled," the cartridge did not say. The module hummed. Somewhere behind the wall the pump kept its one long note, the note Vega had woken to and fallen asleep to since month two, the note that had registered before any voice did, and that Vega now understood was the only reason the voice on the regular calls sounded like a visitor.

The ground called every four days. "How are you holding up?" they asked, meaning the numbers: sleep, bone density, mood scale from one to seven. The ISS had a leak in the water recycler, so Dana Okafor was spending her third week on the station learning to drink her coffee through a valve that smelled faintly of pennies. Nobody had told her that would be the thing she missed about Earth: a mug that tasted like nothing but coffee.

Mission Control called every morning at 06:40 Houston time, which put it at mid-afternoon in the Pacific. She knew this because she had worked it out on the first day and then stopped needing to. Her husband Tomas called on Sundays, when the signal was good and he could wake up early enough to have her full attention. Her sister sent photos of her kids' science fair projects through the cargo-upload queue, two days late, so every drawing of a volcano arrived already slightly out of date.

What nobody warned her about was the window in the Node 3 cupola. She had expected to be awed by the planet. She was, for the first hour. After that the planet became a weather report. She could tell from orbit whether it was raining over Lagos or Lima, and she caught herself wanting to know whether the woman who ran the bakery on her block still put out the sourdough at five.

On the forty-first day, a boy in a village she could not name sent a video through a relief-agency partnership, and it was played in the crew quarters during a stretch of routine. He was standing in a field with a kite made from a grain sack and a bamboo frame, and he was furious at it. The kite kept nosing into the grass. He kicked it. He picked it up, adjusted a strip of tape, and threw it again. On the fourth throw it caught. He yelled something she could not understand, and then the video cut.

She played it four times. Then she went to the cupola, floated to the glass, and found the place where the dark coast of somewhere was rising into morning. She did not look for anything in particular. She just let the frustration and then the catch sit in her chest for a while, the way you let a song you do not like finish playing because stopping it would be a decision.

On the Sunday call Tomas asked how she was doing, and she told him about the kite. He laughed at the right moment and asked if she had sent a reply. She had not. She did not know the boy's name. She did not know what language he spoke. She was not sure what she would even say.

"Tell him it flew," Tomas said.

She sent the message that afternoon, through the same partnership: one line, in English, with a photo of the cupola window taken at the exact moment the coast had come into light. Then she went back to fixing the valve, and the coffee, when she drank it, tasted of pennies and something warm underneath, which was as close to home as she was going to get for another four months.

The badge printed with the wrong first name, and nobody had noticed, so Tomasz wore it all morning. Nobody was going to correct him, he decided. Maybe that was the company's culture.

The lab smelled of burnt coffee and the faint sweetness of the cleaning solution they used on the fume hoods. His desk was a bench by the window with a dead succulent on it, which the previous occupant had left behind, or which had been put there as a test. He moved it to the windowsill. It seemed better to keep it alive than to get rid of it.

Dorota, his supervisor, showed him how to label sample tubes. Her hand-lettering was small and upright, the letters leaning on each other like people at a bus stop. "Date, initials, the batch number, and then the thing you think it is," she said. "Not the thing you hope it is."

By eleven he had labeled forty tubes and gotten two wrong. By noon he had learned that the centrifuge had a personality: it shuddered on the left side and hummed a flat note when it was happy. A technician named Hal told him that the thing to watch for was the note changing pitch. "It's like a kettle," Hal said. "You don't watch the kettle, you listen for it."

At lunch he ate at his bench because he didn't know where else to go. Through the wall he could hear the freezer's compressor cycling on and off, a soft exhale every eleven minutes or so. He timed it on his phone without quite meaning to.

In the afternoon Dorota asked him to run the plate reader. The instructions were on a laminated card taped to the machine, with a coffee ring over the third step. He read them twice, then a third time, because the fourth step said *do not press start until the lamp has warmed*, and he couldn't tell how long that was. He stood there. The machine clicked and began its quiet warm-up.

He waited, and felt the particular dread of the new: that everyone else knew the duration of things, and he was the only one counting.

Then Hal came past with a stack of petri dishes, glanced at the screen, and said, "Ten minutes, roughly. Go get yourself a glass of water. It's not going anywhere."

Tomasz got the water. When he came back the plate reader was humming its flat, happy note, and the first row of numbers was already appearing on the screen, one at a time, like someone arriving at a party.

At five the room emptied slowly. Dorota stopped at his bench on her way out. She looked at the succulent on the sill, then at him.

"The badge," she said. "They got your name wrong."

"I know," he said. "I wasn't sure whether to mention it."

She nodded, as if this were the correct answer, and wrote something on a sticky note. She pressed it onto the edge of his monitor. It said, in the small upright hand: *Ask me tomorrow. Bring the right name.*

He went home with the note still stuck to the bezel of his screen, and the lab's quiet exhale of compressors and kettles stayed with him all the way to the bus stop.

The sea keeps no ledger.
It takes the glass bottle, the child's shoe,
the letter sealed in wax, and gives back
only salt on the lip and a crust of foam
that dries to a map no one can read.

At four in the morning the tide is a clerk
counting what the moon has moved:
two inches of sand, a shell gone,
a rope of kelp laid down like a question
the land forgot to ask.

We build our houses on the edge of this
and call the edge our own.
The water does not argue.
It returns each evening to the same
careful refusal, and the wall of it goes white.

**RUBBER BAND**

It goes missing. It always goes missing. You put one around a bundle of pens and a week later it lives on the floor behind the fridge, stretched into a shape that will never hold anything again.

Good.

A rubber band is the only thing in your kitchen that's honest about its own death. It dries out, it snaps, it gets thrown away — and every time it snapped, it was holding something that stayed shut. Leftovers. A bag of chips. A drawer that would otherwise have opened on a cascade of batteries and birthday candles.

No charging port. No app. No subscription. It costs almost nothing, it does one thing, and it will not last. That's not a flaw. That's the entire deal.

A box of five hundred is about two dollars. Some fraction of them will vanish into the house, which is fine, that's how it works. The rest will do the job while quietly turning to garbage.

**Rubber bands. Around longer than you'd think, gone sooner than you'd like. That's the point.**

*Five hundred count. Natural rubber. Available in the drawer.*

The badge printed with the wrong first name, so for the first hour at Harlan & Pike Freight Forwarding, Nkechi was "Nkeki."

She didn't correct it. Ellis from accounts had printed it, and Ellis was already apologizing for the coffee machine, which had been broken since March and had, he said, a personality. He walked her past the cubicle farm, the window that didn't open, the plant on the fourth desk that somebody had watered so carefully it had drowned.

"Dispatch is through there," he said. "Don't go in. They're at four screens and they hate you by default."

She went in.

Dispatch was six people and a whiteboard covered in a grid of trucks, ports and times. A man with reading glasses on his forehead looked up, looked at her badge, looked back at the whiteboard.

"Nkeki," he said.

"Nkechi."

"Right. Sorry." He pushed a chair toward her with his foot. "Desmond. Sit. The Rotterdam reefer is nine hours late and the consignee thinks we lost it on purpose."

She sat. For three hours she watched him talk to drivers, to a port in Antwerp, to a woman named Priya who ran customs paperwork and swore at the phone in two languages. He never raised his voice. When a driver said there was no way he could make the window, Desmond said, "Tell me where you are," and then, after a long silence on the line, "Okay. Go to the Shell on Route 9. Get the eggs. I'll call them." He hung up. Nkechi said, "What eggs?" and Desmond said, "The eggs he'll be eating if he doesn't sleep, and I'm not having that on my conscience."

At noon she took her sandwich to the stairwell because nobody had told her where lunch was. Ellis found her there.

"You can eat with us," he said. "Or you can eat here. It's fine. Everybody eats here the first week."

"Is everybody eating here?"

"No. Mostly it's the people who were rude to Desmond on the phone."

She laughed, which surprised her, and it made her realize she had been holding her shoulders up since six that morning.

In the afternoon they gave her a login and a queue: forty-one shipment records missing delivery confirmations. The job was boring in the way she had hoped for. Match the scan to the manifest, flag the gap, move on. By four o'clock she had cleared nine and was beginning to feel she had a shape here, a small place in a large, badly ventilated machine.

At five the building emptied in waves. Desmond stood up from dispatch, took his glasses off his forehead, looked at the whiteboard for a long moment, and crossed out one truck.

"Rotterdam's in," he said, to nobody. Then he turned. "Nkeki."

"Nkechi."

"Nkechi. Tomorrow, get the badge fixed. Then get a coffee from the place on Ninth. The machine is a liar."

"I know," she said. "Ellis told me."

"Ellis tells everybody that." He picked up his coat. "He's right, though."

She took the badge off its clip, looked at the wrong name for a while, and put it in her bag to take home. It was, she thought, a good thing to have something to bring back.

The mail allowance for the Meridian station is four hundred grams per crew member per resupply, and Dana Okoye had been the one to weigh it for six years.

Most of it was paper that had to go up. Letters from spouses, a child's drawing folded into quarters, a bag of the sour candy from a shop in Lagos that the commander, Ruth Adair, had asked for in a message nobody could quite explain. Dana weighed each item on the old scale in the back room, wrote the number in pencil on the manifest, and crossed out the things that didn't fit.

Ruth's mail had always been light. Dana noticed it the way you notice a clock that has stopped ticking in a room you still walk through. Two letters from a sister in Ohio, both short. A postcard of a lake nobody on the crew had seen. Nothing else in three years.

On the Tuesday before the launch window, Dana got to the bottom of the bin and found an envelope with no return address. It was thick. She turned it over. The flap wasn't sealed, only tucked.

The rule was clear. Anything not on the manifest stayed on the ground, and anything unsealed was opened by mission security at the far end, which meant it would be read by a stranger in a room with a window onto nothing. She knew this. She also knew the scale read four hundred and twelve grams with the envelope on it, and that the allowance was four hundred, and that the difference was the weight of a single sheet of paper.

She took out the sheet. It was a list in a child's handwriting: the names of every street on the block, with one thing written beside each. *The dog that barks at the mailman. The tree that lost a branch in March. The bakery that gives out day-olds on Fridays.* Forty-one lines. At the bottom, in larger letters: *Come home and tell us which of these you miss.*

Dana stood there longer than the job allowed. Then she folded the list back into its envelope, wrote the weight on the manifest, and marked the bag as cleared. Four hundred grams, exactly. The scale did not know the difference.

The launch went up the next week in weather that was perfect and cold. Dana watched from the observation deck with her hands in her pockets. She didn't know what Ruth would do with the list, or whether she would read it on the first day or the hundredth, or whether it would make the long quiet easier or only heavier.

She had weighed a great many things over six years. This was the first one she had let through by accident on purpose, and she found, to her surprise, that it did not feel like a crime. It felt like the only accurate entry she had made.

Dana weighed each item on the old scale in the back room, wrote the number in pencil on the manifest, and crossed out the things that didn't fit.

Ruth's mail had always been light. Dana noticed it the way you notice a clock that has stopped ticking in a room you still walk through. Two letters from a sister in Ohio, both short. A postcard of a lake nobody on the crew had seen. Nothing else in three years.

On the Tuesday before the launch window, Dana got to the bottom of the bin and found an envelope with no return address. It was thick. She turned it over. The flap wasn't sealed, only tucked.

The rule was clear. Anything not on the manifest stayed on the ground, and anything unsealed was opened by mission security at the far end, which meant it would be read by a stranger in a room with a window onto nothing. She knew this. She also knew the scale read four hundred and twelve grams with the envelope on it, and that the allowance was four hundred, and that the difference was the weight of a single sheet of paper.

She took out the sheet. It was a list in a child's handwriting: the names of every street on the block, with one thing written beside each. *The dog that barks at the mailman. The tree that lost a branch in March. The bakery that gives out day-olds on Fridays.* Forty-one lines. At the bottom, in larger letters: *Come home and tell us which of these you miss.*

Dana stood there longer than the job allowed. Then she folded the list back into its envelope, wrote the weight on the manifest, and marked the bag as cleared. Four hundred grams, exactly. The scale did not know the difference.

The launch went up the next week in weather that was perfect and cold. Dana watched from the observation deck with her hands in her pockets. She didn't know what Ruth would do with the list, or whether she would read it on the first day or the hundredth, or whether it would make the long quiet easier or only heavier.

She had weighed a great many things over six years. This was the first one she had let through by accident on purpose, and she found, to her surprise, that it did not feel like a crime. It felt like the only accurate entry she had made.
</final>

There were three kinds of days in the station. Busy ones, when Earth had questions. Empty ones. And the ones where she cut.

Voss laid the instruments out the way she had been taught the year she turned thirty: scalpel, forceps, the small retractor she had never liked because of the grip. The tray was magnetized. Everything aboard was magnetized or strapped or soft, and after four hundred days her hands had learned to move in the slow weighted box that was not falling.

She had practiced the cut two thousand times across two decades and never once on a person who was breathing. Trays of fruit, mostly. Foam she had cast into little abdomens. Since the launch she had done it on the pale rubber torso bolted to the wall of the lab, twice a week, and marked the date on a strip of tape with a pencil because the pencil still worked and she liked that it did.

The torso had a seam at the collarbone from the mold. She had learned to ignore the seam, which was the first skill, and then she had learned to ignore that it was there, which was the second.

She made the first incision. It had gone smooth. It always went smooth. It was the closing that had started to bother her.

Voss did the closing twice and then a third time, and the third was worse than the second, and the second was worse than the first. The stitch was supposed to sit like a small tooth on the skin. Hers sat like a break in a line. She unpicked it with the forceps, one loop at a time, and found, holding the loose thread, that she had stopped being able to tell the wrong one from the right one by looking. She laid her two hands side by side, palm down, and watched them. The right one was a little stiffer. That was all. That was enough.

Nobody had warned her. Or they had, the flight surgeon, in the year of tests, a hundred pages of the body coming apart in weights it did not evolve for. But the pages were about bone and sleep and the shape the heart took when it was asked to beat a long way from home. Nobody had put down the thing that a hand does in the small slow hours, going a shade foreign, working always under gloves, no one to take the needle from her, no one to say *that's enough, that's beautiful, put it down.*

She ran the mission backwards from her hands.

Hands gone, and then she was a woman alone on a station she could have been launched to with no hands at all, watching the panels breathe, feeding the soil trays, taking the call from the ground that came at the same green margin on the screen. Earth would ask how she slept. She would say fine. That was the whole of it, and Earth would not know from the numbers, because the numbers were all fine. Nothing was failing. Only her hands.

She went out to watch for the capsule. It was not due, and there was no capsule, and this was the only time she had allowed herself to invent a fact, and she allowed it once, and stood at the cupola, and did not say the word *alone* to herself, because saying it changed nothing, and because the window was doing what it did. The Earth went under her, blue and bright and indifferent as a coin. Three quarters of it water. Seven billion hands inside it. Not one that could take a needle away from her at the second stitch.

Inside, the pencil was in the tray, where she had left it, the tape on the wall a row of little dates. She wiped the rubber torso with alcohol and put the instruments back in their channels in the right order, the scalpel last, because she wanted to hold it while she decided whether to write it down. In the end she wrote down the date, and on the next line: *closing continues to require double-check.* There was no second party to sign it.

She put the pencil down, and because the tray was magnetized, it stayed where she left it, not rolling, not falling, holding still under her two hands in that small weighted nothing the station was.

The Thursday log was the only one Dana Okafor found hard to fill in.

Mission Control, Houston, Ground Support Desk 4. Crew check-in, Station Ops, Commander Ilse Varga, 3 minutes 40 seconds. Subject: coffee maker, aft module, status unchanged. Subject: resupply manifest, two items deferred. Subject: weather.

She had never been told to log weather. It had come in during her second month on the desk, when Varga, after the manifest, had asked, almost as an afterthought, whether it was raining in Lisbon. Dana had said she didn't know. Varga had said, "Okay," and then, "Would you look?" So Dana had looked, and reported it, and the next Thursday Varga asked again, and it had become a thing, the way small things become things on a station where nothing else changes.

Lisbon. Then Reykjavik. Then Tbilisi, which Varga had said was where her mother grew up, though she never said anything else about her mother.

Dana kept a separate file, which was against policy. In it she wrote down the forecasts, the wind, whether the photos were bright or grey, because she thought someday Varga might want to see what she had been looking at, and because it seemed unfair that the only one who ever kept track of the sky over those cities was a woman three hundred kilometers up.

The coffee maker was a different matter. It had been broken for nineteen days. Dana had put in the work order twice, and both times it had been deferred behind something with a larger number attached, a pump, a sensor, a part that would ride up on the next supply run. Varga never complained. She only mentioned, every few weeks, that she had started drinking the tea that came in the foil packs, and that it tasted, she said, like a memory of tea.

On the Thursday in question, the check-in ran long. Varga went through the manifest, then the schedule, then said nothing for four seconds, which on a live link felt like a long time.

"Dana, can I ask you something off-log?"

"Sure."

"Is there a way to stop the recording and not have it be a thing?"

Dana's hand moved to the panel before she had decided to move it. The audio light went amber. "Off-log," she said. "It's just us."

"Okay." Another pause. Dana could hear the fan in the station behind her, the faint tick of something cooling. "The rain in Tbilisi. Did you see it?"

"It's dry there today. Thirteen degrees. Clear."

"Good," Varga said. "That's good." And then, so quietly that Dana almost lost it under the fan: "Would you tell me the next one too? Even if it's boring. Even if I didn't ask."

"I'll put it at the top of every log."

"Thank you."

The link closed. Dana sat for a while with the amber light gone and the log half done, the cursor blinking after the word weather.

She did not put the forecast for Tbilisi in the official entry. She put it in the other file, with the date and a single line: she asked me to keep going. Then, because the policy said nothing about this and she had no one to ask, she opened a new work order, filed it under the coffee maker, and wrote in the description field: priority, human. The system would reject that. She submitted it anyway.

Friday morning, Tbilisi was overcast with a light wind off the mountains. Dana checked it twice. Then she typed the number into the first line of the check-in, ahead of everything, the way she had been asked to.

By four o'clock the new hire had been in the building for nine hours and had not yet touched anything that mattered, which Odile considered a good sign. People who touched things on day one broke them on day two.

His name was Tomasz, or Tom, he had said both, and he had a badge that still had its plastic film on the photo, so the security desk had to peel it for him. Odile had watched him stand in the lobby doing the thing new people did, reading the directory board as if a stranger's name might explain the company.

She took him down the back corridor to the lost-property room because that was where she took everyone. It was not on the tour. The tour went past the atrium, the coffee bar with the broken espresso machine that the facilities team had been "looking into" for three years, and the wall of framed awards nobody could name the year of.

The room smelled of dust and cardboard. Shelves ran floor to ceiling, and on them, in plastic bins with masking tape labels, were the things people had left behind: umbrellas, a single glove, a ring box with no ring, a kid's drawing of a horse folded into quarters, a set of car keys on a faded lanyard that said *Rhodes Regional Sales, 2011*.

"Most of it goes in the bin in six months," Odile said. "That's the rule. The rule is the rule."

Tomasz nodded in the way people nodded when they had not yet decided whether a rule was a joke.

"But you don't throw out the keys," he said. He was looking at the lanyard.

"No."

"Why not?"

She had been asked this once before, by a man named Pell who had worked on the fourth floor and who had, the week before he retired, come down looking for a key to a cabinet he had locked in 1998. She had given him the key. He had cried in a way that embarrassed them both, and she had understood then that the room was not really about objects.

"Because someone might come back for them," she said. "Or someone might need to know they existed."

She showed him the forms. Lost-item log, chain of custody, the little yellow sticker for anything with value over fifty pounds. He filled in the first one wrong, writing the date in the wrong box, and she did not correct him. She let him finish and then turned the page so he could see the error and fix it himself. He fixed it. Good.

At half past four the building began emptying in the way buildings did, floor by floor, the lifts groaning their last trips. She could hear it through the walls.

"Do they all know each other?" Tomasz asked.

"Some do. Most know the names of people on their own floor. Nobody learns the whole building, not in a day, not in a year."

"Then how do you know who to give things back to?"

She picked up a glove from the bin, examined the stitching, and set it on the shelf again.

"Usually they come back and tell us what they're missing," she said. "They always come back. It's the ones who don't come back that I think about."

He was quiet for a while. Then he said, "I think I'd like to come back tomorrow."

"Good," Odile said. "Then you'll need to learn the shelf numbers. Everything's coded. And when someone asks you for something you can't find, don't say no. Say you'll look. Then look."

She turned off the light over the desk and left the door ajar, the way she always did, in case someone else arrived looking for something they had lost.

Tomasz stood a moment in the dark before he followed her out.

Nadia gets there forty minutes early, which is the whole trick, the thing she has been doing since she was nineteen. An empty office tells you everything. The coat rack leans. The good chairs have arms. The mail cart stops where the mail cart stops, and you can read a whole department off that.

She waits in the lobby with the lanyard in her pocket, unclipped, because a lanyard around your neck before nine looks like a child playing office. At 8:52 a man comes through with a box of pastries and holds the door for her with his elbow, and she says thank you and learns his name is Bram and that he arrives before the pastries do, which means he is either senior or he has nowhere else to be.

Her desk has a phone with a sticker on the receiver that someone peeled halfway and gave up on. There is a mug, clean, upside down on a napkin. There is a drawer with a ruler in it. That is all. The drawer with the ruler is the best information she has had all morning: whoever sat here left in a hurry, and no one has needed a ruler since, and the desk was cleaned by someone who does not know what a desk needs.

Her manager, Doreen, talks to her for six minutes and says onboarding will be sorted by Thursday, and that she should shadow Priya, and that the team is like a family, and Nadia says mm, which is the correct amount to say. Nadia knows about families. She has been in eleven of them since she was nineteen.

Priya explains the ticketing system, then the real ticketing system, which is that when the Almeida account calls, you just fix it, and the ticket is a story you write afterward about what you did. Nadia writes that down. Priya watches her write it down and something in her face loosens, the way people's faces do when they find out you are going to be useful and not a project.

At lunch Nadia sits with the team and does not say where she is from. Twice. Two different people ask, and twice she gives a place that isn't unkind, that has weather, that they can picture, that is near enough to the truth to be loading a backpack at the right hour. The trick is not lying. The trick is being tired of the real answer, which she is.

In the afternoon she is left alone with the Almeida account for twenty minutes and solves it in nine. She does not say it took nine. She says it was fiddly, and Priya says it's always fiddly, and Nadia feels the small clean click of a room where she could be fine.

At 5:31, after everyone else, she opens the drawer and takes the ruler out and looks at it, a nothing object, twelve inches, six and a half old coffee rings on it. She thinks: you had this desk. You left the sticker on the phone. You did not take your ruler. She doesn't know what happened to whoever sat here and never will, but she knows they did not leave properly, and nobody noticed, and the mug came out of a cupboard for her anyway and was set upside down, waiting.

She puts the ruler back. She clips the lanyard on for the walk to the elevator, because the building is badge-only after six, and this is the part she is good at. The doors closing. The new floor going up or down. The whole stretched second where the day is still undecided and could still go anywhere, and she gets to have it all over again tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after, and she is not going to think about that tonight.

At the corner she turns left, toward a place she hasn't put a bed in yet, and behind her the office windows go on making their light.

<final>Nadia gets there forty minutes early, which is the whole trick, the thing she has been doing since she was nineteen. An empty office tells you everything. The coat rack leans. The good chairs have arms. The mail cart stops where the mail cart stops, and you can read a whole department off that.

She waits in the lobby with the lanyard in her pocket, unclipped, because a lanyard around your neck before nine looks like a child playing office. At 8:52 a man comes through with a box of pastries and holds the door for her with his elbow, and she says thank you and learns his name is Bram and that he arrives before the pastries do, which means he is either senior or he has nowhere else to be.

Her desk has a phone with a sticker on the receiver that someone peeled halfway and gave up on. There is a mug, clean, upside down on a napkin. There is a drawer with a ruler in it. That is all. The drawer with the ruler is the best information she has had all morning: whoever sat here left in a hurry, and no one has needed a ruler since, and the desk was cleaned by someone who does not know what a desk needs.

Her manager, Doreen, talks to her for six minutes and says onboarding will be sorted by Thursday, and that she should shadow Priya, and that the team is like a family, and Nadia says mm, which is the correct amount to say. Nadia knows about families. She has been in eleven of them since she was nineteen.

Priya explains the ticketing system, then the real ticketing system, which is that when the Almeida account calls, you just fix it, and the ticket is a story you write afterward about what you did. Nadia writes that down. Priya watches her write it down and something in her face loosens, the way people's faces do when they find out you are going to be useful and not a project.

At lunch Nadia sits with the team and does not say where she is from. Twice. Two different people ask, and twice she gives a place that isn't unkind, that has weather, that they can picture, that is near enough to the truth to be loading a backpack at the right hour. The trick is not lying. The trick is being tired of the real answer, which she is.

In the afternoon she is left alone with the Almeida account for twenty minutes and solves it in nine. She does not say it took nine. She says it was fiddly, and Priya says it's always fiddly, and Nadia feels the small clean click of a room where she could be fine.

At 5:31, after everyone else, she opens the drawer and takes the ruler out and looks at it, a nothing object, twelve inches, six and a half old coffee rings on it. She thinks: you had this desk. You left the sticker on the phone. You did not take your ruler. She doesn't know what happened to whoever sat here and never will, but she knows they did not leave properly, and nobody noticed, and the mug came out of a cupboard for her anyway and was set upside down, waiting.

She puts the ruler back. She clips the lanyard on for the walk to the elevator, because the building is badge-only after six, and this is the part she is good at. The doors closing. The new floor going up or down. The whole stretched second where the day is still undecided and could still go anywhere, and she gets to have it all over again tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after, and she is not going to think about that tonight.

At the corner she turns left, toward a place she hasn't put a bed in yet, and behind her the office windows go on making their light.</final>

The new one arrived at 7:40, twenty minutes early, which Dorothy had done too, eleven years ago, and which she now understood as a thing people do when they don't know yet how the day is shaped. She had the laminator warming. She always warmed it first, even on days nothing needed laminating, because it took nine minutes and there was no use pretending otherwise.

"Here," Dorothy said, and gave her the sheet with the schedule on it. "Read the board. If you can read my writing, you can do the job."

The new one — Marisol, though Dorothy would not use the name for a week, out of a superstition she could not defend — bent over the whiteboard with her head tilted. Dorothy watched her mouth move slightly. Everyone did that. Nobody said so.

"Tuesday's not a real day," Dorothy said. "Nothing gets done Tuesdays. If someone tells you Tuesday, they mean Wednesday."

"Okay," Marisol said, writing it down, which was wrong, and also fine.

The morning went the way mornings went. Dorothy showed her the drawer where the toner lived and the drawer where the toner was supposed to live. She showed her the machine that jammed if you looked at it and the machine that jammed if you didn't. She said, "You'll learn which is which," and did not say which was which, because that was the training, and the training was not something you could hand someone.

At eleven, the manager came by and said, "How's she doing," about Marisol, to Dorothy, with Marisol standing right there.

"Fine," Dorothy said.

"Good, good," the manager said, and left, and the three of them had all understood something none of them would say.

At lunch Dorothy ate her sandwich in the back room with the radio on low. Marisol ate hers at the front counter because she hadn't been told yet that the back room was where you ate. Dorothy could have told her. She watched her through the window instead, the new one chewing, looking at her phone, at the door, at the parking lot. Twenty minutes. Then she came back and stood by the laminator like it was a post she'd been assigned.

"They let you sit," Dorothy said.

"I know," Marisol said, and didn't.

The afternoon was the rush, the way the afternoon always was, and for two hours Dorothy forgot to teach and just worked, and Marisol worked beside her, and it was almost good, the way two people can be almost good when there's too much to do and no time to be careful. Marisol made two mistakes. Dorothy fixed them before anyone saw. She didn't mention it. She'd had someone do that for her once and had never been able to thank them because she'd never known.

At five-forty the manager came back and said, "Same time tomorrow?"

Marisol looked at Dorothy. Dorothy was doing the register, or the thing you do to the register at the end of the day that isn't quite the register. She didn't look up. She said, "Seven-forty's fine. Seven-fifty's late."

"Seven-forty," Marisol said.

She left. The bell on the door did its thing. Dorothy finished the register, turned off the laminator, and stood for a moment in the noise the building made when it was empty, which was not silence, exactly, but close enough that she knew the difference. Then she got her coat.

On the way out she looked at the whiteboard, at her own handwriting, Tuesday crossed out, Wednesday circled twice, and under it, in the new, careful, wrong handwriting, a line she hadn't put there: *Tuesday is not a real day.*

The badge printer had my name spelled two ways. The lanyard version said Marisol. The plastic card said Marisol too, but the plastic was printed in a font that made the S look like a five, so it read Mari5ol, and nobody noticed but me, and I decided within the first four minutes that I would not be the kind of employee who mentions it.

The woman from HR walked me past the good coffee and the bad coffee and told me which was which without labeling them, which meant I'd have to remember. She said my team sat on the third floor. She said the third floor had its own culture.

It did. The third floor was beige and quiet and full of people watching other people work.

That was the job. I'd known it when I applied, in the abstract way you know things, but the abstract way does not prepare you for a desk with three monitors facing you, one showing the main floor of a store four hundred miles away, one showing the loading dock of the same store, one showing nothing yet because my login hadn't come through.

"Regional Observation," the woman from HR said, like it was a department and not a verb.

My supervisor was a man named Dov, who had been doing this for eleven years and had the calm of someone who had stopped expecting anything from anyone, including himself. He showed me how to log an event. He said the trick was not to log too much. He said a good observer is a good editor. He said he'd once worked a whole shift watching a man stack boxes and had written two sentences about it and both were right.

"Two sentences," I said.

"One of them was 'He is careful.'" He shrugged. "That's a lot, about a person."

The screens were live. The main floor had a checkout girl with a ponytail who kept tucking it back with the same two fingers. A customer spent a long time reading the back of a bottle and then bought a different bottle. The loading dock was empty, and then it wasn't, and a truck that was running late was running late in a way that made everyone on the dock move faster and talk less, and I understood that I was supposed to write this down, and I did, and it was boring, and it was the point.

At lunch I sat alone in the break room because Dov ate at his desk. There was a microwave with a note taped to it that said PLEASE and then nothing after PLEASE, and I looked at that note for a while, the way I was learning to look at things.

The afternoon was worse, because the checkout girl's shift ended and a girl with a ponytail like hers came on, and they stood next to each other for about a second and a half passing the drawer, and in that second and a half the first one said something with her face that I could not read, and the second one made a sound I couldn't hear, and I logged it, because it was an event, and I didn't know what it meant.

Dov read my log at the end of the day. He read it the way you read a receipt, top to bottom, no expression.

"You put the two of them in," he said.

"They were both in."

He nodded slowly, the way people nod when they're deciding whether to explain something.

"The first one's been here four months. The second one started Tuesday." He set the page down. "You wrote about a handoff. That's a good thing to write about. But you've got the two of them as though they're the same kind of person, and they're not, and the difference is the whole story."

I asked what the difference was.

He looked at the screens. The loading dock was lit up like a stage. Somebody was moving a pallet, badly, and another person was standing with their hands on their hips watching him do it, and none of this had anything to do with me.

"Wednesday you'll see it," he said. "Go home."

I went home. On the bus I caught myself watching a man argue with a parking meter and thinking, without meaning to, He is careful. He is not careful. And it occurred to me that this was the job, that I had already started, and that tomorrow there would be more of it, and the day after that I would stop being new, and I would be the one who could tell a handoff from a handoff.

**The spoon is still here.**

Everything else went out with the move. The kettle with the cracked lid. The pans that warped on the left-hand burner. The blender whose blades you took out in 2009 and never put back.

The spoon stayed. It was in the drawer by the sink, where it always is, and it did what it has always done: pushed the onions around the pan without scorching them, scraped the good brown bits up off the bottom, and didn't leave a single scratch on the non-stick.

Nobody buys a wooden spoon to be noticed. You buy it, and then, for years, you forget it is there, which is how you know it is working.

Plain beech. Hand-finished. Made to be used until the grain softens under your thumb.

Keep one for the things you'll be making for a long time.

Nobody has ever asked the sponge how it is.

It lives on the edge of the sink, in a little puddle, between the dish soap and the cloth nobody remembers buying. It gets the pan with the cheese stuck to it. It gets the ring a mug left on the wood. It gets the thing you pretend you did not see on the plate, and then it gets the rest of the plate.

Nobody notices when it is doing well. Nobody notices when it is not, either, until the smell arrives on Tuesday.

So here is a small thing to do this week. Squeeze it out. Run the tap over it. Turn it over in your hand and see the thick, yellow, worn-down edge it has become. That is not a failure. That is the job, done properly, for a long time, without a single thank-you.

Replace it when it has earned the bin. Keep one in reserve, dry, in the drawer.

Kitchen sponge. Unglamorous. Right where you left it.

**The Doorstop**

A doorstop looks like it's fighting the door. It isn't.

A wedge holds because of the door, not against it. The weight that's trying to close on you is the same weight pressing the wedge down into the floor, and the harder the door pushes, the harder the wedge grips. It gets stronger the more you lean on it.

That's the whole trick. It's why a doorstop the size of your palm can hold a door that weighs forty pounds, and why it never needs to be screwed in, glued down, or explained.

Most things in a house that hold a door open are trying to be clever — magnets, hooks, little arms that snap. They work until the floor is wrong, or the door is heavy, or someone's hands are full.

This one works because the door is trying to close. Let it.

*Doorstop. Wood, one angle, no instructions.*

1. **Deposit-splitting for people with thin credit files.** Rental deposits assume a lump sum, which locks out anyone paid weekly — the exact people landlords say they want but screen out. This fronts the deposit as a monthly line item with the landlord named on it, so the tenant builds a payment record that is actually usable in the next application.

2. **A scheduling tool built for home health aides, not clinics.** Aides juggle three or four agencies and get paid per visit, so a canceled shift is unpaid time they only learn about by text. This treats the aide as the customer: one calendar across all agencies, with a logged record of every cancellation they can take to the agency or the labor board.

3. **Commercial-grade wifi for laundromats and barbershops.** A laundromat's customers sit for 45 minutes, and that is a captive audience no advertiser can currently reach, because the buildings have terrible connectivity and no one sells to them. Sell the router cheap, run the screen on the machines, and split the ad revenue with the owner — the audience already exists; they are just sitting there bored.

4. **A parts broker for independent appliance repair.** Manufacturers stopped selling diagnostic software and certain parts to independent techs, which pushes customers into buying new machines or waiting weeks for a company tech. The broker sources refurbished boards and aftermarket diagnostics from the gray market and clears the legal line, letting a $180 repair compete with an $800 replacement.

5. **Payroll built for the tip-pooled shift.** Restaurants, salons and bars legally require tip pooling, but the split math is done on a spreadsheet by whoever is least likely to complain — and it is usually wrong in someone's favor. This computes the split from the POS and the schedule, shows every worker their own share, and keeps the record an owner needs when the state asks.

If I had to pick one: **#4**. The customers have money, the pain is structural (they cannot legally buy the fix), and the wedge is supply, not adoption — you do not have to teach anyone to want it.

final: In the drowned city of Harrow's Reach, every bell that rings underwater belongs to a debt owed to the sea, and Nell Varrick, a diver who recovers the bronze bells for scrap, has been paying hers in silence for nine years. When a bell she salvaged starts ringing on dry land, the sea's creditors come calling: a tide-priest who wants the bell back, a smuggler who wants to sell the debt to the highest bidder, and her own brother, who drowned at sea and is now walking the harbor wall. Nell must decide whether to pay the sea, sell the bell, or learn to ring it herself, a choice that would reveal the price her family has been secretly paying for the city's bread. Sweeping, salt-stained, and intimate, this is a fantasy about inheritance, obligation, and the quiet costs of a comfortable life.

final: In the salt-cured port of Venn Hallow, the lighthouse keeper's daughter, Marisol Tev, discovers that the beacon she has tended for nine years does not guide ships home. It calls the drowned dead back to the shore, one lantern-lit night at a time, and the town has been quietly paying the tithe of its own grief to keep it burning. When Marisol tries to snuff the light, the dead begin to knock on the doors of the people who signed the old bargain, starting with her mother. Told in alternating chapters from Marisol's cramped lighthouse journal and the ledger of the town's richest family, the story turns on a single question: is a sea-thin mourning worth a town's whole memory of its losses, and who gets to decide when to stop paying?
