It was meant to call something up from beneath the harbor, and it has been keeping it asleep. When the lamp begins to fail and the first drowned bells start ringing from the seabed, Odile must recruit the reluctant guild of tide-clerks, who record every flood in ledgers no one reads, to reconstruct the city's forgotten bargain with the deep before the sea decides to collect on it. Told through the ledgers themselves and Odile's increasingly unreliable logbook, the novel asks who gets to decide what a city owes its own drowned past, and whether the only honest keeper of a promise is the one who was never asked to make it.

final: A century ago the empire solved magic. Not how to make it — everyone can make it, a farmer can curse his own field, a child can unmake a wasp — but how to *measure* it, and measuring it turned out to be the same as owning it. Every spell anyone casts now draws on a shared ledger, and the ledger has a limit, and the limit is enforced by the Ration: an office of clerks who decide, in advance, how much magic each district, guild and household is permitted to spend, and who have never once in a hundred years had to explain where the unspent remainder goes. Sera Vane is a third-grade actuary in that office, good at her job, the kind of person who can look at a family's petition for two more units and tell you, without cruelty, exactly why they don't need it. Then she finds a discrepancy — a rounding error, four hundredths of a unit, recurring monthly for sixty years — and follows it down through the ledgers until she understands what the Ration really is: not a limit, but a *faucet*, and the empire has been quietly drinking the difference for six generations while teaching its citizens that the well is going dry. She has no sword, no prophecy, and no standing to accuse anyone of anything. What she has is the paperwork, and the fact that the only way to prove the theft is to commit one, and the fact that the man who taught her to read a ledger is the one holding the tap.

1. **Pharmacy-grade dosing for home-dialysis patients.** Many people on home dialysis must track fluid and electrolyte intake by hand, and a simple app that converts their daily meals into safe allowances, flagged for their nephrologist, could cut hospital readmissions. Start with the clinics that already run home-dialysis training programs.

2. **Shift-based childcare matching for hospital and warehouse workers.** Parents working overnight or rotating shifts often cannot find care that starts at 5 a.m. or runs past 10 p.m., and a marketplace of vetted home caregivers booked by the hour could fill that gap. Begin in logistics hubs and hospital districts where shift schedules are predictable.

3. **Repair and resale of mid-range appliances for landlords of small rental portfolios.** Owners of two to ten rental units rarely get the bulk service contracts large property managers do, so they pay premium rates or live with broken equipment. A subscription service that handles repairs and replacements across a small portfolio would fill that gap.

4. **Accessible translation of government forms for recent immigrants.** Official forms for benefits, permits and tax filings are often written at a reading level and in a format that excludes people who are fluent in everyday English but not in bureaucratic language. A tool that produces plain-language, field-by-field guidance in the user's own language, reviewed by certified translators, could reduce missed deadlines and rejected applications.

5. **Booking and reminder software for independent tutors of students with learning differences.** Specialist tutors for dyslexia, ADHD and dyscalculia typically run on paper calendars and personal spreadsheets, and general scheduling tools ignore their need for session notes, progress tracking and parent reporting. A purpose-built tool for these tutors would save them administrative hours and make their work easier to show to families and schools.

1. **Pharmacy-linked pet medication delivery for rural owners.** Many farms and rural homes are a long drive from a vet or clinic that stocks the prescription a pet needs, so this service would pair a regional courier network with telehealth prescribing and ship medication on a fixed refill schedule. Veterinary clinics in low-density areas would get new prescription volume without expanding their storefronts.

2. **Shared-use commercial kitchens for home bakers in regions with strict food rules.** Home cooks who want to sell baked goods often hit local rules that bar home production, yet they cannot afford a full commercial lease. The product would be a membership-based, hourly-booked kitchen network that handles permits, inspection-ready equipment, and bulk ingredient purchasing for small producers.

3. **Scheduling software for independent sign-language interpreters.** Freelance interpreters often juggle bookings through email, text, and spreadsheets, and deaf clients have little say in how appointments are matched or confirmed. A booking platform built with deaf users and interpreters together could handle multi-day assignments, credential tracking, and video-based confirmation in the user's preferred language.

4. **Repair-and-return service for mobility aids such as wheelchairs and walkers.** Owners of these devices often wait weeks for repairs or end up replacing a whole unit over a worn part, and small local repair shops rarely have parts on hand. A service that collects, repairs, and redelivers devices through a network of partner technicians would extend device life and cut out-of-pocket costs for people on fixed incomes.

5. **Seasonal staffing marketplace for small-town hospitality and agriculture.** Rural inns, orchards, and processing plants need short-term workers at predictable times of year, but local job boards are fragmented and rarely reach people who travel for work. The business would run a verified worker pool that follows the harvest and tourism calendar, handling housing listings, pay tracking, and onboarding in one place.

The sea does not remember being new.
It has been rain, and been the inside
of a stone, and been the blood
of something walking, and come back.

Nothing in it is original.
The wave that breaks tonight
has broken before, somewhere,
under a different wind, and will again.

It is not lonely and it is not deep.
It is busy: lifting, letting go, lifting,
the way a person folds a sheet
that will only need folding again.

We came late. We stand at the edge
with our small bags of water
and call it endless, because we are short,
and because we want something
to have been here always.

It was. That is the trouble. It does not
need us to say so. It goes on
sorting the light, keeping
the salt where it belongs, waiting

to be the rain again,
to be the tap, the cup,
the hand that turns the tap off,
the mouth.

Assumption: I'm reading "underserved market" as people whose problem is real and routine but who are unglamorous to sell to — not a demographic that's merely underrepresented in ads. Each idea names that population and the structural reason they're ignored.

1. **Freight-lane rest-stop dentistry.** Long-haul drivers lose teeth on the road because dentistry requires a fixed address and a booking made weeks out; a mobile clinic that parks where trucks already stop overnight fits their actual life instead of asking them to change it. Why here: the barrier isn't cost, it's that the service assumes a schedule truckers don't have.

2. **Inventory for the corner shop that can't count.** Tiny groceries run on gut feel and lose real money to spoilage and stockouts, but every inventory product is priced and designed for chains; a phone-camera tool that only needs a shelf photo and speaks the owner's language would sell to the 90% the incumbents skip. Why here: the underserved aren't small chains, they're one-person shops below the minimum viable customer for existing software.

3. **A school-run logistics co-op for parents who share custody.** Divorced and separated parents coordinate drop-offs over text and shared calendars that don't handle two households, and the failure is a kid standing outside a locked gate; a simple custody-aware schedule that both parents can edit, with the handoff as the unit rather than the day, solves a problem no family app takes seriously. Why here: the market is large and the pain is sharp, but it's invisible to products built for the nuclear-family default.

4. **Death paperwork as a service for the people left holding it.** After a death, someone spends 40 to 100 hours closing accounts, canceling subscriptions, and filing with agencies, usually while grieving and often without legal training; a guided service that does the sequencing for them treats the survivor, not the estate, as the customer. Why here: estate lawyers serve the estate; nobody sells to the exhausted person doing the work.

5. **Shift-worker banking that runs at 4 a.m.** Nurses, plant workers and warehouse staff get paid and spend on schedules that don't match banking hours or the "9-to-5 direct deposit" assumption baked into most fintech onboarding; a bank built around irregular pay cycles and overnight hours wins a customer base everyone else treats as an edge case. Why here: it's a timing mismatch, not a wealth mismatch — the money is there, the hours aren't.

My pick: **#3**, because the pain is frequent, the buyer is easy to reach through schools, and the failure mode (a child left waiting) is the kind of concrete harm that makes word-of-mouth spread fast.

1. **Estate-access service for the unbanked.** Roughly a third of US adults have no will and no executor, and when they die their family can't reach the phone, the bank, or the storage unit. A dead-man's-switch that releases a curated packet of account credentials and instructions to one named person, priced at a one-time fee, sold through funeral homes and credit unions rather than direct to consumers.

2. **Renter-stability insurance for long tenancies.** Renters who stay put for years are the cheapest tenants a landlord can have, yet nothing rewards them and every lease renewal is a fresh threat. A product that pays the tenant a cash bonus at each renewal milestone and funds it by selling the landlord a lower-vacancy guarantee.

3. **SSA-contribution recovery for undocumented workers.** Millions of people pay payroll taxes under someone else's or an invalid number and can never claim the benefits they funded. A nonprofit-adjacent service that reconstructs a person's contribution record from pay stubs and W-2s and files for the refund or credit where immigration status allows it.

4. **Shift-worker childcare that starts at 4 a.m.** Nurses, warehouse crews and bakers need care at hours no daycare center opens, so they rely on unpaid relatives and lose shifts. A licensed overnight and pre-dawn care network staffed by people already awake at those hours, sold as a monthly subscription through hospital and logistics employers.

5. **Tools for the people who clean up after everyone else.** Hospice aides, crime-scene cleaners, and shelter staff handle the physical aftermath of events the rest of us only read about, and they buy their own supplies, gloves and decontamination gear out of pocket. A bulk-ordering and training cooperative owned by the workers, with purchasing power and certifications they can't get alone.

Assumption: you want commercially viable ideas for markets that are large but rarely sold to directly, not charity pitches.

final: A century ago the empire solved magic the way it solved water: it made it a utility. Now every spell in the realm draws on the same reserve, metered, taxed, and maintained by the Unhoused — people who owe more spell-debt than they can ever pay, indentured to the grid that keeps the lamps lit and the wards standing. Sera Voss is a repairwoman who climbs into the conduits nobody else will touch, and she has just found the reserve is not infinite; it is something alive, and it is nearly out. The empire's answer is to ration it — which means choosing which provinces go dark, which wards fail, which debts get forgiven and which get called in. Sera has one advantage the throne does not know about: she can hear the thing in the reserve, and it has started asking her questions. To keep the lights on she will have to decide who deserves them, and every answer she gives is a name someone will die by. It is a story about infrastructure, love that looks like an unpaid bill, and the terrible arithmetic of a civilization that made its magic someone else's problem.

The problem was the chair. Not the mission, not the two years, not the way his legs had forgotten what down meant. The chair. He sat in it at 4 a.m. because he couldn't sleep and couldn't stand the bed, and the chair was the only thing in the house that didn't expect him to be doing something.

For a while he'd done the talking. Everyone wanted the talking. The man from the agency with the good haircut, the doctors with their clipboards, his sister on the phone from Phoenix saying *tell me the good parts.* So he told them: the silence up there, the way the station ticked when the sun crossed it, how a screwdriver floats if you aren't watching. They ate it up. He got good at the good parts.

The parts he kept: that he'd stopped recognizing his own voice in the recordings, that the screen conversations with his daughter had a lag he learned to live inside, that near the end he'd started talking to the ship the way you talk to a dog in a room you thought was empty.

She was eleven when he left. Fourteen now. She'd written him a message every week — he'd read them, he'd answered, mostly from range, the words just tired enough not to hurt. Then he came home, and the messages stopped, because what was there to write when someone was in the next room.

He picked up the phone four times that first month. Dialed, listened to it ring once, hung up. Not because he didn't want to. Because he didn't know which voice to use — the one that had been piped through speakers, or the one he hadn't heard out loud since before.

His sister called on a Tuesday. She said, *She thinks you don't want to see her.* He said that wasn't it. His sister waited. He said it again. She said, *Then what is it,* and he couldn't answer, because the answer was a chair at 4 a.m. and the way the lag had gone both directions.

So he did the small thing. Not the phone. He wrote it down, the way he'd learned to write messages up there when every word had to survive the trip. He kept it to what would fit. He put it under her door at his sister's house, where the girl was staying, and then he went outside and sat on the step facing the street, which on Earth meant one thing only.

The note said: *I got used to loving you from far away and I forgot the sound of you up close. Give me a minute. I'm coming.*

He sat on the step for a long time. He didn't know if the door would open.

It did.

**Desmond Okonkwo — The Witness Who Remembers Everything and Believes None of It**

Desmond has hyperthymesia: he can replay nearly every day of his life, in order, in full. He remembers what he wore, what was said, the exact pause before the lie. He remembers it all so vividly and so involuntarily that he's spent twenty years learning what memory researchers have been saying for decades — that vividness and truth are not the same thing. He has testified in eleven trials. Nine convictions. Two men exonerated by DNA. Both had been identified by Desmond himself, with total confidence, from a memory as clear as a photograph.

So Desmond does not trust his own eyes. He works cases backwards. When someone says "I saw a man with a red scarf," Desmond asks: what were you *trying* to see? He is a forensic memory consultant for the public defender's office, and his specialty is dismantling eyewitnesses, including — especially — himself. He founded an organization that reviews confidence-based identifications, and its first published case study was his own: *Okonkwo, D., State v. Reyes, misidentification.*

He has one rule: if he is certain, he is dangerous.

**The mystery he's built to solve.** A murder at a family reunion. Twenty-three relatives, all with clear accounts, all mutually corroborating. Every witness agrees. That unanimity is the clue no one else reads — a murder solved by the fact that nobody is uncertain. Desmond's investigation isn't "which of the twenty-three is lying." It's "how many of them are telling the truth about a night that didn't happen."

**The flaw that isn't a superpower.** He can't forget any of it — not the two exonerations, not their faces as each was led out, not the exact pitch of his own voice saying "that's him." He can't blur anything, not even the parts that should blur. The mystery with the answer he's most afraid of is the one already stored in his head.

**Why here:** a memory consultant for the public defender's office has every reason to distrust certainty — the brief's genre demands a mind that can be both the instrument and the crime scene. The "reliable everyman" detective who trusts his own account is precisely the trope a story about misidentification should invert.

Success is not a place you arrive at and put your bags down. It is the morning you do not want to get up, and getting up anyway.

You will not feel ready. Readiness is not a prerequisite; it is a rumor.

There is no day you become the final version of yourself. There is today, and the work today asks for, and the choice to be a little less of a stranger to the person you are trying to become.

Keep your dreams where you can reach them, in front of you, unglamorous, unposted. Pick them up on the days you would rather not. That is the whole trick, and it is not a trick at all.

You do not have to believe in yourself to start. Start, and belief catches up.

Think of the internet as a postal system for messages that never travel in one piece.

Suppose you want to send your aunt a long letter, but the post office has a rule: no envelope may be heavier than a teaspoon. So you cut the letter into small slips, number each one, and mail them separately. The slips go out through different post offices, some take the fast road and some the slow one, and some arrive out of order. When the slips reach your aunt's door, a clerk there lays them in sequence, checks that none are missing, and hands her the whole letter. Nobody needed to send the slips in order. They only needed the numbers.

That is roughly what happens when you open a web page. The page is cut into small packets of information, each one marked with where it came from and where it is going. Each packet passes through a chain of relay stations, each one reading only the address on the outside and passing it on toward its destination. No single station knows the whole letter, and no single station is in charge. If one route is blocked, the packets find another.

The addresses matter. Every computer connected to the internet has a number, like a house number on a street. When you type the name of a website, a kind of directory, a bit like a phone book, turns that name into the number the packets need. Your request goes out, the far-off computer that holds the page receives it, and it sends its own packets back to you. The page appears on your screen as those pieces arrive and are put in order.

So the internet is not one big machine or one wire. It is an enormous, loosely cooperating network of post offices, all agreeing on the same rules for numbering, addressing and passing along small slips, so that a letter can be torn apart, mailed in pieces by many routes, and rebuilt on the other side.

Suppose you want to send your aunt a long letter, but the post office has a rule: no envelope may be heavier than a teaspoon. So you cut the letter into small slips, number each one, and mail them separately. The slips go out through different post offices, some take the fast road and some the slow one, and some arrive out of order. When the slips reach your aunt's door, a clerk there lays them in sequence, checks that none are missing, and hands her the whole letter. Nobody needed to send the slips in order. They only needed the numbers.

That is roughly what happens when you open a web page. The page is cut into small packets of information, each one marked with where it came from and where it is going. Each packet passes through a chain of relay stations, each one reading only the address on the outside and passing it on toward its destination. No single station knows the whole letter, and no single station is in charge. If one route is blocked, the packets find another.

The addresses matter. Every computer connected to the internet has a number, like a house number on a street. When you type the name of a website, a kind of directory, a bit like a phone book, turns that name into the number the packets need. Your request goes out, the far-off computer that holds the page receives it, and it sends its own packets back to you. The page appears on your screen as those pieces arrive and are put in order.

So the internet is not one big machine or one wire. It is an enormous, loosely cooperating network of post offices, all agreeing on the same rules for numbering, addressing and passing along small slips, so that a letter can be torn apart, mailed in pieces by many routes, and rebuilt on the other side.
</final>

**Ruth Abernathy-Osei** writes parking tickets on Calder Street, the same four blocks, six days a week, for nineteen years. She keeps a notebook she has never shown anyone: a column for every car that parks there regularly, with the make, the colour, the hour it usually arrives, and the hour it leaves. It is not a crime-solving tool. It is the habit of a woman who likes to know what should be where.

She is not brilliant in any way that would make a film. She is slow to decide and quick to notice. When a car is out of pattern, she feels it the way you feel a step that isn't there.

The mystery begins on a Tuesday, when the grey Volvo that has parked outside the closed dry cleaner every weekday since March does not arrive. Ruth writes that down, because it is what she writes down. By Thursday it has not come back, and a second car, a dark green hatchback, has been sitting outside the dry cleaner's back door from 2 a.m. to 4 a.m. for three nights running. Nobody on Calder Street has noticed. Ruth has, and she has no standing to care: she is not a police officer, and the only thing she is entitled to do is issue a ticket.

So she writes the ticket. Then she writes a second note, to the one person she has ever heard say a kind word about the dry cleaner's late owner, and the mystery opens from there.

What makes Ruth useful is not her memory of faces. It is that she is the only person in the neighbourhood who has been paid, for nineteen years, to look at the same street every day and ask whether it is right. The people she is trying to catch assume that no one is looking at them at all. That assumption is the flaw she is best placed to exploit.

**Protagonist: Wendell Prue, Senior Claims Adjuster, Brightwater Mutual**

He works out of a booth, not an office. Claims come to him as paper: a proof-of-loss form, a police report, a repair estimate, a photograph of a stairwell with the middle step painted a slightly different color. His job is to decide whether the story attached to the money is true. He is very good at it. He has never once been called a detective, and would be annoyed by the word.

What makes him work as a mystery protagonist: he arrives after the fact, on purpose. Everyone at the scene (if there is a scene) has already agreed what happened; his only tool is the small seam where the versions don't line up. A widow says her husband fell down the basement stairs. The police report agrees. The railing has been repainted, but only above the fourth step, the height a hand grips when it's pulled, not when it's leaned on. Wendell notices because noticing is how he pays his mortgage.

His method is bureaucratic, and it produces the story's engine: he can't arrest anyone, can't search a house, can't compel a word. He can only ask questions that a man with a payout on the line has to answer, and then wait. Then he writes a recommendation, and the recommendation either releases the money or refuses it. In a small town, a refused payout is louder than an arrest. People come to him. People send him things they shouldn't. Somebody's brother-in-law knows where he parks.

Where the friction lives: Wendell is not brave. He's careful. He has a bad shoulder and a lunch he eats at his desk. He would like nothing more than a clean file in the drawer by four. But a clean file now and then isn't clean, and the part of him that can't leave it alone is the same part that costs him everything else. His ex-wife works at the county clerk's office and still pulls records for him, out of habit and grudge.

The first case that finds him: a fire at a farm-supply warehouse that Brightwater would rather just pay. The file is thin. The fire marshal's report is short. Wendell's own signature is already on the reserve, dated three days before the fire.

Think of the internet as a postal system for messages that never have to travel as one piece.

Suppose you want to send your grandmother a long letter, but the postal system only moves envelopes through a single road, and the road is jammed. So you cut the letter into dozens of numbered slips, each with the address written on it. The slips go into different vans, and each van takes whatever route is open at the moment. Some slips arrive early, some late, one might take the long way around a closed bridge. At her house, a worker lays the slips out in order by their numbers, reads the whole letter, and hands it to her. If a slip gets lost, she sends a note asking for it again, and only that one slip is resent.

Now replace the vans with cables, radio signals and wires under the ground. Replace the numbered slips with "packets," small pieces of your message, each with its address and order number. Replace the sorting worker with the computer at the other end, which reassembles everything.

The "address" is the part that makes it work. Every device connected to the internet has one, a string of numbers that tells the network where it is, the way a house number tells a mail carrier where to deliver. When you type a name like a website's address into your device, something acts like a phone book, turning that name into the numbers the network actually uses. That phone book is itself spread across many offices, so no single one has to know everything.

The web, the part you see when you open a browser, is one particular way of using this postal system. A website is a set of letters kept at a fixed address, waiting for anyone to ask for them. When you click a link, your device sends a request ("please send me the letter at this address"), the request travels through the network as packets, the far-away computer sends its reply back the same way, and your browser lays the pieces out on your screen as a page.

So the next time you look at a photo sent from across the world, picture it as a letter cut into a thousand slips, delivered by whichever van was free, reassembled in order, and handed to you in less time than it takes to blink.

Marguerite Oyelaran had served lunch at Halvorsen Elementary for nineteen years, and in that time she had learned that nobody looks at the woman with the ladle. They look at the clock, the milk cartons, the child who is crying. They do not look at who knows how many tomatoes went into the sauce, or which fourth-grader has been sneaking a second tray for three weeks, or why the vice principal's account at the bank next door is always thirty dollars short on Thursdays.

So when Dr. Penhallow was found in the supply closet with a paring knife in his back and a half-eaten pudding cup in his hand, the detectives set up in the staff room and asked everyone where they had been between eleven and twelve.

"Serving," Marguerite said, and the detective, a young man named Rourke with the careful posture of someone who had been told to be patient with civilians, wrote it down.

"Can anyone confirm that?"

"Two hundred and twelve trays," she said. "Plus the four extra for the staff who skipped breakfast. I count the trays. The count is always the same unless someone is lying about being hungry, and I can tell you which of them is lying."

He looked up, not quite smiling.

She had kept the ledger for the cafeteria account since before the school had a computer. Every free-lunch ticket, every cash top-up, every child whose balance went quietly negative and was quietly covered by a card she never signed. She knew that Penhallow had been moving the cafeteria's surplus, two hundred dollars a month, into a line item labelled "nutrition outreach," and that the outreach was a company whose address was a post office box in Dayton. She had told no one. A ladle does not accuse the chef.

"The pudding," Rourke said. "He had a pudding cup. Do you know whose it would be?"

Marguerite turned it over in her mind the way she would a suspicious invoice. Chocolate, the brand that came in cases of forty-eight. Penhallow was lactose intolerant, everybody knew, because he complained loudly every Friday that there was no oat milk, and yet he had been carrying a pudding cup into a closet at eleven forty. Someone had put it in his hand. Someone wanted the pudding to say something.

"He didn't eat them," she said. "He never ate the dessert. He gave his to Dariusz Kowal, the boy in Room 9, who gets two desserts because his father does not sign the forms and I do not ask him to. If that pudding is his, the dead man was feeding a boy he was supposed to be starving, and somebody needed you to think the dead man ate his own dessert."

Rourke set down his pen.

"Who would need that?"

"Somebody who knows the ledger," said Marguerite, and went back to counting trays.

final: Every spell in the Vaulted Cities is borrowed against a life, and the ledger only balances if somebody dies on schedule — so the empire runs on actuaries. Sera Quill is one: a clerk who calculates how many years a healing costs, who signs the receipts when a farmer's fever is paid for with his daughter's sixtieth birthday. She is very good at it, right up to the morning the ledger names her own mother as collateral for a drought that hasn't happened yet, and the arithmetic stops being arithmetic. To void the debt she has to trace where that entry came from — through moneylenders who trade in decades, a guild of saints who are actually collection agents, and the one creditor the Cities have never managed to foreclose on, who has been patient for six hundred years and is now, finally, sending a reminder. It is a heist novel where the thing stolen is a number, and the getaway is the rest of a life.

**The Sorter at Halden Street Laundry**

Dorota Wren has sorted other people's clothes for nineteen years, and in that time she has learned that nobody's shirt is ever as clean as they say it is.

The night shift at Halden Street runs from ten to six. Four machines, two dryers that rattle when they are overloaded, and the long steel table where Dorota stands with a tray of wet cotton and her reading glasses pushed up into her hair. Her hands know the work. Her eyes go where the work does not need them.

On the third Tuesday of March, a man named Peter Abell brought in a navy overcoat with a split inside the left pocket. The lining was torn the way a hand tears it when it is looking for something, not the way a coat tears from wear. Dorota turned the coat over twice before she put it on the rail.

"Lost something?" asked Ilse, who worked the folding table and liked to talk through the shift.

"Somebody did," Dorota said. "Not him."

She went through the pockets with the seriousness she gave everything. A ticket stub for the Lantern Cinema, two days old. A little curl of dry grass. A receipt from a pharmacy on the far side of the river, paid in cash, timed 9:14 p.m. The grass was the thing she kept looking at. It was the kind that grows only in the gap by the railway embankment, where the council sprays but the spray never reaches.

Abell came back at six for his coat. He was pleasant. He called her "love" and asked after her knee. She handed him the coat and said nothing about the lining.

That afternoon she took the bus out past the embankment and walked the gap with her hands in her cardigan. Two hours on her feet, which her knee did not forgive. She found what she expected to find: a scrap of cinema card half-buried by the ballast, and a patch of ground where something heavy had been dragged and then swept, badly, with a branch.

She went home, put the kettle on, and rang the number on the card in her coat pocket. It was the Lantern's lost property. The woman who answered had a wet cough and no time.

"A girl came in Sunday," the woman said. "Asked about a ticket. Said her sister had been to the late show and never came home."

"What was her sister's name?"

"Hang on."

Dorota waited, and the kettle began to tick as it cooled.

Tomorrow night the coats would come in again. She would be at the steel table at ten, sleeves rolled, glasses in her hair, reading the cloth the way other people read faces. People always assumed the clean things were the honest ones. In nineteen years Dorota had found that the dirty ones told her more, provided someone was willing to look past the stains and ask where they came from.

Imagine you want to read a letter your friend wrote, but your friend lives in a city you have never visited, and you have never met them.

Start with the address. Every computer connected to the internet has one, a string of numbers that works like a house number on a street. When you type a website's name into your device, a kind of directory (like a phone book kept by the postal service) turns that name into the number of the house where the website lives. You are not sending your request to a place you can see. You are sending it to an address.

Now the letter. Your request, something like "please send me the page called News," is written on a sheet of paper. But the postal service does not send the sheet whole. It tears the message into small envelopes of equal size, a few hundred words each, and writes on every one the destination address, the sender's return address, and a number showing its place in the order, say envelope 3 of 7. Each envelope is called a packet.

The envelopes are then handed to the nearest sorting office. The sorting office does not know the whole route. It only knows which next office is most likely to bring each envelope closer to its destination. So envelope 1 might travel through three offices in one city, envelope 2 through a completely different set of offices, and envelope 3 through a third. Some arrive early, some late, and a few get rerouted around a jammed office. No single office holds the whole letter, and no one needs to.

At the far end, the website's own building receives the envelopes, checks the numbers to make sure none are missing, and puts them back in order. It reads the request and writes a reply, which it splits into envelopes too, and posts them back using the return addresses. The same thing happens in reverse, through whatever offices are working best at that moment.

That is the whole trick. Every message is cut into numbered pieces, each piece carries its own address, and each sorting office only passes pieces along toward the next step. Your news page arrives on your screen as a letter reassembled from envelopes that may have taken completely different paths, and within a fraction of a second, so quickly that the postal workers never seem to hurry.

Think of a very large village where nobody ever travels.

Everyone lives in a small house with a locked door. In each house there is a shelf, and on the shelf sits whatever that person keeps: a photograph, a letter, a list of the people they know.

In the middle of the village stands one enormous library. It holds a copy of every shelf in every house, and it never closes. That library is the internet. Your computer is just your house, and your shelf is the small part of the library that belongs to you.

Now, the library has an odd rule. It will not let you walk in and take a book. Instead, every house has a clerk who works for you and never sleeps. You tell the clerk what you want — a page, a picture, the price of a train ticket — and the clerk runs to the library, finds it, copies it, and puts the copy on your shelf. The original never leaves the building. That is why you can look at the same photograph as a million other people at the same moment without it running out.

To ask for something, you have to give the clerk an address. Every shelf and every page in the library has one, and it is exact: not "the train timetable" but which timetable, in which drawer, on which floor. If you give the address slightly wrong, the clerk comes back empty-handed or brings the wrong thing. When people say a page "doesn't load", that is usually all that has happened.

When you send something out — a note to your sister — the clerk does not hand it to her clerk. She has her own address, so your note is written out in full, put in an envelope, and carried across the village to her house, where it is copied onto her shelf. She reads it whenever she opens the door. That is why she can read it at midnight while you are asleep: the journey already happened without either of you.

And the village is not one road. It is a web of roads with a great many junctions. Any note can take any of several routes, and if one road is blocked the note simply goes another way. That is the whole reason the thing keeps working when parts of it break: there was never only one way to get anywhere.

The last thing to know is who owns what. The library building is not owned by anyone in particular, and no single person runs it. But each shelf is somebody's, and many of the shelves belong to businesses that pay for the space, which is why some of them are loud with posters and some ask you for money. You are not walking through a building. You are sitting in your own house, and a clerk is bringing the village to your shelf, one request at a time.

Imagine a neighborhood where nobody drives across town. Instead, everything anyone wants to send gets written on a small card, sealed in a little envelope, and handed to a neighbor.

Here's the odd part: your long letter doesn't travel as one letter. It gets cut into dozens of little cards, and each card is sent off on its own. Card 7 might go down Elm Street. Card 8 might go around by the river. They take completely different routes. Some get delayed. Some get handed back and sent again a different way. But each card has a tiny label — where it started, where it's going, and its number in the stack — so the person at the other end can lay them all out and rebuild your letter exactly.

Now, who decides the routes? Nobody. That's the strange, important thing. There's no mayor of this neighborhood, no central office, no boss handing out directions. Each person who receives an envelope just looks at the label and passes it to whoever they think is a step closer. That's all they know. They don't know what's in the envelope, and they don't know the whole route. They just know their one small job: get it one step nearer. Somehow, out of thousands of people each doing only that, your letter arrives.

And it isn't just houses. It's shops and offices and libraries, all connected by these hand-offs. Some places are big sorting rooms stacked with envelopes, open all day and night, passing along millions of cards an hour. Others are just one person's kitchen table.

When you want something — a picture, a song, the answer to a question — you don't go get it. You send out a request: a little card that says "please send me the picture at this address." It gets chopped up and passed along the same way. The place that has the picture sends it back the same way, in pieces, by whatever routes are open. Your table reassembles it, and there it is. That's all "loading" is: waiting for the cards to finish arriving.

Two more things make it work. First, everyone follows the same simple rules for labeling and passing, so a person in one town and a person in another can hand off to each other without ever having met. Second, because there's no one in charge and no single road, it keeps working even when parts break. If a route floods, the cards just go around. You'd only notice something was wrong if an awful lot of roads flooded at once.

So the internet is not one big machine and not one big pipe. It's a huge number of ordinary connections, each one small, each one only knowing its next step, adding up to a way for anything at all to reach anywhere.

Reason: the brief's core difficulty is that beginners imagine one big pipe or one big machine; the analogy must make "chopped into pieces, each finding its own way, reassembled at the end" feel ordinary. Keep it concrete, no jargon leaks, no invented facts presented as claims.

<final>
Imagine a neighborhood where nobody drives across town. Instead, everything anyone wants to send gets written on a small card, sealed in a little envelope, and handed to a neighbor.

Here's the odd part: your long letter doesn't travel as one letter. It gets cut into dozens of little cards, and each card is sent off on its own. Card 7 might go down Elm Street. Card 8 might go around by the river. They take completely different routes. Some get delayed. Some get handed back and sent again a different way. But each card has a tiny label — where it started, where it's going, and its number in the stack — so the person at the other end can lay them all out and rebuild your letter exactly.

Now, who decides the routes? Nobody. That's the strange, important thing. There's no mayor of this neighborhood, no central office, no boss handing out directions. Each person who receives an envelope just looks at the label and passes it to whoever they think is a step closer. That's all they know. They don't know what's in the envelope, and they don't know the whole route. They just know their one small job: get it one step nearer. Somehow, out of thousands of people each doing only that, your letter arrives.

And it isn't just houses. It's shops and offices and libraries, all connected by these hand-offs. Some places are big sorting rooms stacked with envelopes, open all day and night, passing along millions of cards an hour. Others are just one person's kitchen table.

When you want something — a picture, a song, the answer to a question — you don't go get it. You send out a request: a little card that says "please send me the picture at this address." It gets chopped up and passed along the same way. The place that has the picture sends it back the same way, in pieces, by whatever routes are open. Your table reassembles it, and there it is. That's all "loading" is: waiting for the cards to finish arriving.

Two more things make it work. First, everyone follows the same simple rules for labeling and passing, so a person in one town and a person in another can hand off to each other without ever having met. Second, because there's no one in charge and no single road, it keeps working even when parts break. If a route floods, the cards just go around. You'd only notice something was wrong if an awful lot of roads flooded at once.

So the internet is not one big machine and not one big pipe. It's a huge number of ordinary connections, each one small, each one only knowing its next step, adding up to a way for anything at all to reach anywhere.
</final>

**Vera Okonkwo, 61, decommissioned actuarial investigator — now the woman who writes the "how it happened" paragraph on other people's claims.**

She spent thirty years deciding whether fires were accidents, whether falls were real, whether a body found in a stairwell was a fall at all. Not police. Nobody ever arrested anyone because of her. She just wrote the sentence that decided whether a family got paid, and that sentence was usually right.

She has no gun, no badge, no authority to enter a room. What she has is a nose for the lie that costs the least. Most people lie small. They pad the value, they move the time by ten minutes, they say "he was always careful" about a man they know wasn't. Vera has learned that murderers lie the same way — not dramatically, just conveniently — and that a convenient lie in a claim file looks exactly like a convenient lie in a statement to police, except nobody at the precinct reads claim files.

She works the case because it is her case. The dead woman is a name in a pending claim Vera was quietly about to deny — a payout she'd already decided was inflated by someone who knew the insured was about to die. Denying it would have buried the thing. Approving it would pay the person who did it. So she has to know which, and she is the only one who already read the paperwork that proves it, and she has no standing to say so.

Her method is arithmetic and impatience. She arrives with a clipboard and asks the questions a detective wouldn't think to ask because they don't matter to a conviction: what did the locksmith charge, why is the receipt dated Tuesday when the funeral was Tuesday, who benefits from the *deductible*. She is small, unhurried, and slightly rude. People answer her because she sounds like a bill.

What she wants is not justice. It's a sentence that is true. She has written thousands of false-comfortable ones in her life — for insurers, for widows, for the file — and this is the last one she gets to write, and she would like, once, to be exactly correct.

The flaw: she trusts her own arithmetic over people, and once she has decided what happened, she will bend the small facts to fit the large one. Which is, of course, the same crime she's hunting.

The dock post has known the tide
the way a clock knows nothing,
by being struck, again, and again,
and by staying where it was put.

The snail in the pool goes on
with its one slow errand,
reading the rock for salt,
not once looking up.

Out past the gulls the water
is folding a grey blanket
it has folded every morning
and will fold again for nobody's sake.

By noon the boats have gone to lunch.
The sand is hot enough to stand on
and the ocean, which has no hurry,
leaves a line of shells to say it was here.

At dusk the post and the snail
and the thin bright seam of the horizon
all go dark at the same speed,
which is the only agreement
anyone has ever needed.

**Descent**

No light survives past the first two hundred metres.
What you called blue was only the top of it,
a skin the sun keeps borrowing.

Below, the water holds its cold like a held breath.
Something with no eyes maps the dark by pressure,
feels a whale pass like weather, and does not look up.

The oldest water here fell before the sun was lit
and has been falling since, through the mouths of fish,
through the slow arithmetic of salt.

Nothing down there has a name for the surface.
It simply keeps the weight, and the weight keeps it,
and the drowned mountains wait with their peaks unvisited,

patient as a word no one has needed yet.

The badge printed her name with a typo, Marisol Okonkwo-Reyes shortened to Marisol O-R, and nobody at the front desk seemed to think it mattered. Dana from HR handed it over with a lanyard that was already twisted.

"Your desk is by the window," Dana said. "The window opens. Don't ask why it opens. Nobody knows."

Marisol's desk was a rectangle of gray laminate with a coffee ring in the shape of a boot. Someone had left a single yellow sticky note on the monitor. It said: *Not yours. Don't touch the drawer.*

She did not touch the drawer.

At nine-fifteen a man named Teodor came by with a laptop under one arm and a sandwich in a bag. He sat down across from her without introducing himself, unwrapped the sandwich, and began to type with the sandwich still in his other hand.

"You're on the Pell account," he said, not looking up. "Don't let them tell you it's urgent. It's always urgent. Nothing is ever urgent."

"Okay."

"Also, the printer on this floor is haunted. Print to the one on four."

She wrote *haunted printer, four* on the back of her hand because she had not yet been issued a notebook.

Lunch was a cart in the hallway, selling bananas and a kind of pastry that had been there since before she arrived. She bought a pastry. The woman at the cart said, "First day?" and Marisol said yes, and the woman said, "Good. Eat that. You'll need it by three," and went back to counting coins into a tin.

At three the building had a fire drill that was not a drill, because the alarm went off and then, after forty seconds, a voice over the speakers said, very calmly, "This is not a drill, but it is also not a fire," and everyone kept walking, and Marisol kept walking with them, down the stairwell, into a parking lot that smelled of cut grass. Teodor found her there, sandwich gone, holding her lanyard in both hands.

"Welcome," he said. "That was the one that counts."

She laughed, which surprised her, and then stopped laughing, which surprised her more, because she realized she had not been nervous since the drawer. She could not remember when she had stopped being nervous. Somewhere between the haunted printer and the parking lot.

Back upstairs, the yellow note was still on her monitor. Under *Not yours*, someone had added, in smaller, sloppier handwriting: *Yours now. Good luck.*

She peeled it off, folded it, and put it in her pocket.

Then, very carefully, she opened the drawer.

The Bath

Fill the tub to a green ear.
Lower yourself in.
The ocean is not what you were shown.

You can hear it either way.
The ocean is a sound first:
the tap is the whole Atlantic
finding one tile.

Salt is what it keeps.
Put your tongue to the tap and it comes on the lip,
a smaller moon, brine's own moon,
the taste of a thing that has no edge.

Here the waves are the water you paid for.
It holds you the way the sea holds a hull:
not tenderly. Firmly.
It does the same to the drowned.

Somewhere a tide is being read out
to people who will never stand in it.
A reading. A number. A beach.

Lie back. Let it come over the face.
This is the part of the ocean
that has no seeing in it.

Listen. It is already going out without you.

The lamp was the first thing. It was on the desk, plugged in, and it worked — she tried it before she tried the computer. The cord had been routed through the little hole at the back of the desk and taped down with clear tape gone yellow. Someone had done that on purpose, so they'd always be able to find it. That was a kind of person, she thought. The kind who taped a cord down.

Dana from the third floor showed her the coffee machine and the bathroom and the kitchen with the two jugs, one labeled in marker that was fading. Dana did not answer the question she didn't ask — the desk, the lamp, the name on the lanyard that wasn't hers. She just said the Wi-Fi was on the whiteboard and stood there a beat, then said, "You can put your stuff in the top drawer, or the bottom one, whichever." Like the drawer was a decision. She chose the top one and opened it and there was nothing in it except a folded paper clip chain, six links, and a small thing of lip balm with the wrapper half off.

She didn't throw them out. She thought about it, and then she put her own pens in on the other side and left the chain and the balm where they were, and closed the drawer, and that was the first day.

By lunch she'd learned the passwords were the old guy's birthday, still, because nobody had changed them, and the coffee was the kind you get used to, and Dana had a laugh that carried when you didn't expect it. At 4:50 she was told the last bus was at 5:15, and she took it, and it was the same bus she'd take the rest of the week, and the rest of the month, and she didn't know that yet. She just sat by the window and watched the office recede behind the parking lot, and told herself she would get the lamp out when she quit. She wouldn't, but she told herself.

Every glass of water
has been somewhere
it does not remember.

The tap coughs once,
then gives me the cold
it has been keeping
since the last wave
let go of it,
miles and miles
of salt,
folded down into
a single clean
ordinary thing.

I fill the kettle.
Out past the reservoir,
past the pipes that run
under the road and the river,
the sea is still
doing what it does
without a single witness,
pulling itself back
from the shore
and throwing itself
back again.

Some of it
will come to me
tonight, warm
in a cup,
and I will not taste the ocean,
only the nothing
that water is
when it has been
very far from home
and come back
polite.

The first thing Marisol was handed at Lost & Found was a single red glove, still warm from someone's hand, or so it seemed to her.

"Tag it, bag it, shelve it by the week," said Dev, who ran the back room and had not looked up from his screen since she arrived. "If nobody comes for it in ninety days, it goes to the donation truck on Thursdays. Don't get attached."

She tagged it. The tag said RED GLOVE, LEFT, FOUND HALLWAY 3, 9:14 A.M. She wrote her initials on the bag in careful capitals, the way she had been taught at her old job, where everything had a number and nothing was ever just somewhere.

By eleven she had learned the drawers. Reading glasses in the first one, dozens of them, folded and waiting. A child's sneaker with a cartoon fox on it. A wedding ring that Dev said had come back twice. Keys, always keys. She had started a list in the margin of her notebook, then stopped, because the list was getting longer than the day.

At lunch, a woman from accounts came in with a heavy canvas bag and asked, shyly, whether anyone had turned in an umbrella with a yellow handle. Marisol checked the umbrella rack. Dev said it was in the bin by the door, and it was, and the woman held it for a moment without taking it, as if confirming it was real.

"It rained on the bus," the woman said. "I lost it on the bus, and then I thought, well, that's gone, and then I thought, no. Someone like me might have picked it up."

She took it and left. Marisol stood with her hand still on the rack.

In the afternoon she was asked to sort a box of things that had come in from the staff bathroom: a pen, a hair tie, a crumpled receipt for two coffees on a date in March. She read the receipt twice before she bagged it, though there was nothing to learn from it except that somebody once had a good enough day to buy two coffees. She tagged it anyway. Shelved it anyway.

Near five, Dev finally looked up.

"You're fine, you know," he said. "Most people are a mess the first day. They come in thinking they'll be the one who fixes the place. Then they find out the place is mostly people keeping small things safe until someone shows up."

"Is that the job?" she asked.

"That's about half of it." He went back to his screen. "The other half is the Thursday truck, and you'll hate that part."

She put the red glove back on its shelf, left side, week one, and looked at the tag for a while. Then she went home through the lobby, past the sign-in desk, past the hallway where she had found the glove, and for the first time that day she noticed how many things people lose on the way to being somewhere.

**The Keeper of the Water**

You keep the blueprints of every ship
in a drawer that has never been built.

I imagine you at a desk of drowned light,
lamps of pale kelp, ink that refuses to dry,
writing down the names as they go under —
the *Lady Alice*, the *Bella Rose*,
the one that was only a number.

You do not lose them. That is the trouble.
Nothing is lost down there.
Every boot, every kettle, every letter
opened by salt
sits exactly where it fell,
still saying what it said.

We send you bottles, and you file them.
We send you coins. You file those too.
We drop sonar down your corridors
and you show us the corners
you are willing to have looked at.
The rest is your own business.

I know you are not cruel.
I know the cold that comes off you
is just the cold of a room
where the work is never done.

But when I swim out past my feet,
past where I can see my hands,
I feel the pencil stop,
the small dry pause,
the page turned over.

The job was to collect what people left on their first day, which was, most days, nothing. A cardigan over a chair. A branded mug. A sandwich gone soft in a drawer with a name on it, misspelled. I had a trolley and a key ring and a list of rooms, and by four o'clock the building was a series of small embarrassing proofs that someone had tried.

I'd been told the role was "reset and refresh," which meant put the chair back under the desk and wipe the surface and check the bin. I was good at it by the second week, but I remember the first desk I did, because it was warm, or nearly, the chair turned three-quarters away like the person had just stood up to answer a door. There was a laptop they'd already taken back. There was a mug with an M on it. There was a sticky note, blue, folded in half and left at the edge of the tray like a note passed in class: *ask about the Friday thing, ask about the Friday thing.* Nobody had asked about the Friday thing. That was the whole reason I was there.

The trick, I learned, was not to look at any of it. You took the mug by the handle, you dropped the sandwich, you wiped the ring the mug had left. The room didn't want a witness, it wanted a clean surface. Still, some things don't fit in a bin bag. A photo of a cat on a stick, cut out and taped to the monitor — the monitor was gone. A greeting card, still in its cellophane, *Welcome, Priya*, unopened. A printed page with a table on it and one cell ringed in pen, and under the table the words *this is the only number that matters, don't let them*, and then nothing. I put that one in my pocket. I still don't know why. Maybe because it was folded the same way as the blue note.

By six, every room was a room again. I stood in the last one with my hand on the light switch and looked at the chair, which was straight now, and the tray, which was empty, and it was so clean it looked like nobody had ever been in it, which was the job. The lift went down slowly. In the lobby the security guard was reading a paper and he said, without looking up, "first day, is it," and I said yes, and he said, "you'll be all right, they all leave, it's the ones who don't that worry me," and went back to his paper.

My cardigan was still on the chair in the room where I started. I went back up for it but the lift took ages, and I stood there in the empty lobby holding my key ring, listening to it come down for me, and I thought about the M on the mug and the card nobody opened and the number that mattered, and I thought: you spend one day being new and then you spend years being the thing someone else has to clean up. The lift opened. I didn't get in. I went up the stairs.

The cardigan was on the floor. Someone had moved the chair aside and vacuumed under it, and put everything back wrong — the chair facing the wall, the tray on the wrong end, the whole room faintly crooked, like a photograph hung a little off. I stood in the doorway with my key ring and I recognized it, the way you recognize a thing you did to yourself and then left for someone else to find. I didn't fix it. I took my cardigan and turned off the light and went down the stairs, and on Monday I'd have to start again, on the same floor, from the top.

**Station Log, Orbital Habitat Meridian-7**

**Day 41.** Comms check at 0600. Voice on the line is Okonkwo, the morning controller. He says "Meridian, copy" the way some people fold a shirt: quickly, and with one corner held back. I say "Copy" back. We both know there is a gap between the words where something could be said. Neither of us says it.

**Day 42.** He clears his throat before every fourth sentence. I have counted. Eleven clears in a shift. I wonder if he knows. I wonder if a rule against it exists, or if he just has a throat.

**Day 44.** Mission protocol says controllers may not discuss anything outside the mission. I have no outside. The window is the only outside, and I am instructed not to describe it, because descriptions are "nonessential transmissions." So I describe the solar array temperature instead, which is the most beautiful thing I have looked at all week, and I say it with the same flatness they taught us.

**Day 47.** Okonkwo hums under his breath when the line is open but nobody is talking. I can only hear it when the fan in my suit drops. It is four notes, falling. Then a fifth that does not resolve. He never finishes it. I have started to wait for the fifth note the way you wait for a bus that you know is not coming.

**Day 49.** Logistics: the resupply capsule is late by six hours. Okonkwo apologizes twice. I say it is fine twice. The second time, my voice cracks on the word "fine," and there is a gap on the line I cannot account for, and then he says, "Copy, Meridian," very gently, and I believe he is still there.

**Day 53.** Another controller came on at night. Her cough is wet and she tries to hide it behind the mic. I now know the sound of two strangers' bodies, and I catch myself listening for her to recover. I do not know her name. I am not supposed to ask.

**Day 55.** I asked. Protocol says a name is "identifying information" and I should not have it. Okonkwo, on the morning shift, said nothing for four seconds, then said, "Copy." I think that was a no. I think it was also the most anybody has told me in weeks.

**Day 56.** Okonkwo was off this morning. A new voice. Clean, careful, no throat-clearing. I found myself waiting for the cough. It did not come. I wrote the time down anyway: 0600, no hum, no fifth note.

**Day 57.** Okonkwo is back. He does not mention the gap. At 0612 he hums the four falling notes, quietly, as if he thinks the line is muted. I do not answer. I am listening for the fifth note. I do not think he will finish it. I am writing down that he started.

**Day 58.** Comms check, 0600. "Meridian, copy." "Copy," I say. Then, against procedure, I add one nonessential word, and I do not say what it is, because the log is read by people who are supposed to stay outside it. But I will tell you it was four notes long, and the last one I left open.

The pump on rack four had started clicking the way a person clicks a pen.

Mara heard it from the galley, where she was thawing a pouch of rice. She put the pouch down and went to listen. Two hundred and nine days she'd been on the station, and in that time she had learned the difference between clicking that meant *settling* and clicking that meant *dying*. This one was the second kind. She'd known it since the second click, and she had still stood there for a full minute with her ear near the wall, hoping to be a person who didn't know things.

The rack held eighty-one liters of nutrient solution. In it lived a thin green sheen, cyanobacteria, unremarkable on Earth and the entire reason the station existed. It broke the water, fed the scrubbers, kept the air loose and breathable. Mara's job was to pour and stir and log. Ninety seconds of work, most days. The rest of the day she was free, which on a station meant: free to notice.

She opened the panel. The clicks were coming from the housing, a soft little mechanism working itself apart.

"Okay," she said out loud, because there was a habit of saying things out loud here. "Okay, okay. Okay."

She got the wrench out of its velcro and went to work. The repair took two hours. She cut her thumb. She swore, and the swear floated off through the station, and no one heard it, which was the whole problem, and also not the whole problem.

The whole problem was this. Somewhere below her, four hundred kilometers of water and rock and fog, there was a woman named Itziar who had done this before. Itziar had trained her. Itziar had handed her the pouch of rice on her first morning and said, *The algae will not thank you, and that's the job.* Itziar was dead eleven months now, in an apartment in Zaragoza, of an aneurysm, while Mara was four hundred kilometers up and did not know for four days, because nobody wanted to break it to her over the comms.

Mara had cried up there, once. It was terrible, the crying. The tears just balled up at her lashes and sat there, little warm beads, and would not fall.

She finished the repair. She logged it. *Rack 4 pump. Removed debris. Chris.* She was not Chris. She had done this once before and caught it, and this time she caught it again, and deleted it, and typed *Mara*, and looked at the word.

The scrubbing stopped clicking. The station settled into the small hum it made when it was content, a hum like a house at night with everyone asleep.

She took the pouch of rice out of the galley and ate it standing up, looking through the cupola at the curve of the dark. Not at the Earth, though it was there, blue and ruinously beautiful, the way it was every day. At the dark, past it. Where the other stations were. Where the people were. She thought: someday someone will come up, and I will hand them the rice and the wrench and the log, and I'll say what she said, and it won't be true yet, and then it will be.

She wiped the last of the rice off her thumb with her tongue.

"Okay," she said. And she went to check rack five, which was three racks early, and clicked her pen.

"Okay," she said out loud, because there was a habit of saying things out loud here. "Okay, okay. Okay."

She got the wrench out of its velcro and went to work. The repair took two hours. She cut her thumb. She swore, and the swear floated off through the station, and no one heard it, which was the whole problem, and also not the whole problem.

The whole problem was this. Somewhere below her, four hundred kilometers of water and rock and fog, there was a woman named Itziar who had done this before. Itziar had trained her. Itziar had handed her the pouch of rice on her first morning and said, *The algae will not thank you, and that's the job.* Itziar was dead eleven months now, in an apartment in Zaragoza, of an aneurysm, while Mara was four hundred kilometers up and did not know for four days, because nobody wanted to break it to her over the comms.

Mara had cried up there, once. It was terrible, the crying. The tears just balled up at her lashes and sat there, little warm beads, and would not fall.

She finished the repair. She logged it. *Rack 4 pump. Removed debris. Chris.* She was not Chris. She had done this once before and caught it, and this time she caught it again, and deleted it, and typed *Mara*, and looked at the word.

The scrubbing stopped clicking. The station settled into the small hum it made when it was content, a hum like a house at night with everyone asleep.

She took the pouch of rice out of the galley and ate it standing up, looking through the cupola at the curve of the dark. Not at the Earth, though it was there, blue and ruinously beautiful, the way it was every day. At the dark, past it. Where the other stations were. Where the people were. She thought: someday someone will come up, and I will hand them the rice and the wrench and the log, and I'll say what she said, and it won't be true yet, and then it will be.

She wiped the last of the rice off her thumb with her tongue.

"Okay," she said. And she went to check rack five, which was three racks early, and clicked her pen.
</final>

One assumption: I read "story" as a short one, not a novel chapter — if you want it longer, the material that would expand best is the four days she didn't know about Itziar.

The water recycler on Station Halden hummed at a pitch Mira had stopped hearing in her first month and started hearing again in her fourth. Every morning at 0600 she logged it: 41.2 decibels, a number nobody asked for. The log was hers. She had started it on day one and kept it the way other people keep a diary, except the entries were only numbers, and the numbers were the only part she trusted to be true.

Ninety-one days out. Ninety-one days of 0600 entries, the cabbage seedlings in the corner tray leaning toward the one LED panel that worked, and the small, ridiculous routine of checking the seals on the food locker, then checking them again, because if she checked them twice the locker was a place someone had been.

At 1900 the ground network opened a window. Her name went up on the board, and for twelve minutes there was a voice. The voice belonged to Dov, a flight controller in a windowless room in Houston or Darmstadt or wherever the night shift sat. They had talked on the link for eleven weeks, and neither of them had once asked where the other lived.

"Halden, Ground. Water margin nominal."

"Copy nominal," she said. "Recycler's at forty-one point two."

A pause, long enough to carry a little delay and something else. "Forty-one point two," he repeated. "That's good. That's the number we want."

"It's the number I wrote down."

"Same thing, out here."

She almost laughed. She looked at the seedlings instead, and at the window. Earth was turning under the station, a blue she had given up trying to describe, and she thought of the thirty-one other people who would sit in cramped rooms tonight and watch this same pass on a screen, and how none of them would know what forty-one point two sounded like.

"Dov."

"Yeah."

"Do you ever check the seals twice?"

Another pause. Shorter this time. "Every night," he said. "Front door, back door. Then I go back and check the front door again."

"Why?"

"I don't know." His voice was quieter now, and the delay made it sound like it came from further away than the room it was in. "So the house is somewhere I've been."

Her window ran out at 1912. He said good night, and she said good night, and the board went dark. Mira floated to the food locker, put her hand on the seal, and felt it hold. Then she logged the evening: 41.2 decibels, seedlings up two millimeters, one conversation.

She did not check the seal again. She had someone else who did that, now.

Nadia's first day at the credit union had been going for six hours when Dale told her about the drawer.

"You don't really use it," he said, meaning the top one, the one with a key that had lived in her pocket since nine-fifteen and now had six hours of thumbprint on it. "But the first guy who had this desk, he had this whole thing." Dale did something with his hands that did not clarify anything. "So it's in the drawer."

The drawer was full of file folders, the old kind, with a string that came around a cardboard button like a hair tie. Nadia had been hired to move these folders onto the computer, where they would be findable, which was her job. She had done four folders. There were, by the drawer's own testimony, three more drawers under it, and the file room, which she had peeked into at lunch, had. Well. It had walls.

Her desk was at an angle in the open office so that everyone who walked from the door to the coffee could see her screen, and they had all been very kind about it. Everyone had said some version of welcome. A woman in purple had told her where the good bathroom was, two floors up, and Nadia had thanked her and thought about it all afternoon the way you think about a rung on a ladder.

At eleven, she had gone down to the lobby and stood at the window for four minutes with her badge turned inward, the photo side pressed against her sternum, so nobody passing could see that she was new. It was not really that she was ashamed. It was that the photo made her look like someone with a plan.

Dale's shift ended at three. He put on his coat and stood there with his hand on her chair back, not quite touching it.

"You want to cry in the drawer," he said. "That's what it's for. First guy did."

"Did he."

"He lasted a week. Treasury, that's where he went. He said the drawer thing to me on his first day and I didn't understand it either and you'll do the same to whoever's next." He took his hand off the chair. "You'll be fine. The folders have never had anyone not finish them. That's the thing. People come and go and the folders get done."

After he left, Nadia sat for a minute. Then she unlocked the top drawer and looked in at all of it, the long gray spine of it, lined up, waiting, each folder a person who had once stood at a counter and been told something and signed. Somewhere in the file room were the people she would be thinking about on her lunch break next month, whom she had not met yet and never would, who would arrive in her hands like mail.

She slid the drawer shut and locked it, because the key was hers and there was a whole procedure, and then she did the fifth folder.

It was a refinance. There was a name at the top in blue pen, and under it an amount, and the amount seemed impossibly small, a number you could carry in one hand, and someone had underlined it twice. Nadia typed the name. She typed the amount. She hit enter, and the entry appeared on the screen in front of her, small and dark and findable from anywhere in the building, from any floor, from the good bathroom two floors up.

Her train was in an hour. She did the sixth folder anyway.

By ten they had given her a locker, a lanyard and a tuning fork she was not allowed to strike against anything.

"Against your knee, if you need it," said Mr. Okafor, who ran the workshop and talked mostly to the pianos. "Not against the piano. Pianos don't like to be told things directly."

Her name was Ines. She had spent eleven years restoring furniture for a company that sold it to people who wanted to look like they had restored furniture, and she had come here because someone had told her that in this shop nobody pretended. The shop smelled of hide glue and felt. Eighty-eight keys lay in a tray on the bench like teeth waiting for a dentist.

The piano in the back corner had been brought in six weeks ago. Everyone had tuned it. Everyone had said it was fine.

"It's wrong," said Mr. Okafor. "Listen."

He played a single C. Then a G. Then the C again. Ines heard nothing wrong, and said so, and he nodded as if she had passed a small test by being honest.

"Good. Now the chord. Don't tell me what's wrong. Tell me what the room is doing."

She sat on the bench and played. Three notes, then the same three with the sustain pedal down. The room had a window that rattled faintly when the bus went past on the street. The radiator ticked. A woman two doors away was laughing on the phone. Under all of that, the piano was saying something slightly sideways, a hum that rose and fell against the rattle of the glass.

"The window," she said. "It's sympathetic to the piano. When the bass goes, the glass answers, and the piano answers the glass."

"Yes."

"So it isn't the tuning. The tuning is fine. The room is making it sound wrong."

Mr. Okafor sat down on the next stool. For a while neither of them said anything. Then he picked up a wedge of felt, looked at it, and put it back.

"Most people would retune it," he said. "Then the room would win again in a month."

"What do we do?"

"You move the piano six inches. Or you put a weight on the sill. Or you ask the landlord to fix the window, which he will not do, so you put the weight on the sill." He shrugged. "There is almost never a wrong note. There is only a wrong relationship with the room."

At lunch a man named Dmitri, who had been there nineteen years, showed her where the good kettle was and the bad one. He asked what she had done before and did not look surprised. He told her the workshop had hired four people in the last ten years and kept two. He did not say which two.

After lunch she moved the piano. It took her and Dmitri and a dolly and a great deal of swearing, and when they set it down the window stopped rattling in the chord. Mr. Okafor played the three notes once, then twice, then stopped.

"There," he said. He did not say anything else.

At five, when the light had gone orange on the felt and the kettle was cold, she put the tuning fork back in its case. She had not used it once. She had listened all day, to a room she had walked into that morning as a stranger, and it had told her what was wrong with it, and she had moved the furniture.

On her way out she passed the piano. She pressed the C, very gently, and waited for the window to answer. It did not.

What the Sea Keeps

Coins, mostly, from ships
that went down with their owners' names still on them.
Buttons. A clock stopped at a quarter past nine.
Glass that was a bottle once
and now has the patience of a stone.

It keeps the bones of whales
in a silence so thick the light gives up at two hundred meters
and turns to a rumor, then to nothing.
It keeps a squid the size of a bus
that no one has seen whole.

It keeps the first sound the planet made
and most of the ones after,
folded down under the cold,
pressed flat like flowers in a book
nobody opens.

We stand at the edge in our socks
with a thermos and a towel
and call the grey line the ocean,
the way you'd call the lid of a box the box.

But I have seen the sea give back
one shoe, one tin, one child's red mitten
after forty years,
rinsed and perfectly ordinary,
as if it had only been holding them
for a minute, to be polite.

So go in when you can.
The cold will tell you what you are.
And the sea, which keeps everything,
will keep you a little, too,
and send you back salt-faced and changed,
with something in your pocket you didn't bring.

Nobody has ever been moved to tears by a colander. This one is not trying to change that. It sits in the sink, holds back the pasta, and lets the water go. Forty years from now someone will still be reaching for it without looking, which is the only test an everyday thing needs to pass.

Hold it. The steel is cool at first and then it isn't. The holes are exactly the size they were the last time, and the time before that.

Lift it out of the cupboard and the rim catches on the same chip it always catches on. Pour a full pot through it. Let the steam climb your wrist.

It does not need you to think about it. That is the whole offer.
